paragraphs.text: BOOK ONE.

You often ask me to explain many things in the sacred books that need an interpreter. I will gather together, as they come back to my memory, the questions you, my Salonius, have put to me so diligently and so abundantly in your eagerness to learn. I will answer them not from my own wit but from the judgment of illustrious teachers, not from my own rashness but from the authority of others, aiming not at the sweep of exuberant eloquence but at the measure of necessary brevity. In this way I will be able to satisfy your countless questions, and I will also be free to add some things from outside that I think will be useful for your understanding: for instance, what alleluia, diapsalma and amen mean, or what a cidaris, an ephod and a shekel are, and other such things which either occur frequently in the sacred books or are in very common use in the Church, and so need to be explained. Since these come up again and again for readers throughout the whole body of the Scriptures, I thought it not out of place to show them to you in this work, gathered together, as it were, with their meanings. For it is fitting that I repay your talent with every care I can. You were barely ten years old when you entered the desert, and there you were not only instructed but brought up in the hands of the saints, under father Honoratus — under him, I say, who was first the teacher of the islands and afterwards also of churches. There the teaching of the most blessed Hilary, then a recruit on the island but now a most eminent bishop, shaped you in all the disciplines of spiritual things; and afterwards the holy men Salvian and Vincent, outstanding alike in eloquence and in knowledge, brought you to completion. Having had so many teachers of such quality, you will now hear from me too, the least of all, the answers to what you have asked. In what follows, recognize yourself already as the one asking and me as the one answering. Farewell in Christ.
ON THE MORE DIFFICULT QUESTIONS OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS. ON GENESIS.

By what testimonies of Scripture is the Trinity proved? It is declared, made plain and spread abroad in many ways and with many indications through nearly all the sacred books, but let us show it briefly right at the very beginning of the divine Scriptures. "In the beginning," it says, "God made heaven and earth." And below: "And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters." "In the beginning" means "in the Son," because God the Father made heaven and earth through the Son, to whom the Father also says, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." For he worked all things through the Son, since "all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made." And the Spirit of God that was borne over the waters is, of course, the Holy Spirit. There you have God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Again, another passage: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth." Here are the Lord, his Word and his Holy Spirit. Again in the Gospel: "Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." But the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten. For if we called him unbegotten, we would seem to speak of two Fathers, and if begotten, of two Sons; rather, he is the one who proceeds from the Father and the Son, as a kind of concord of the Father and the Son. Indeed, among us too there can be no true concord without the Holy Spirit. This same Spirit is called both the love of God and the gift of God, and he is also the one who distributes the graces. So the Father is the one from whom are all things, the Son the one through whom are all things, and the Holy Spirit the one in whom are all things, as the apostle also says: "For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever."
How was the Spirit of God borne over the waters?
Not by moving about from place to place but by power, as he rises above his creation with the command of one who rules it.
Where do we read that the waters were made by God?

Even though the text of divine Scripture did not state plainly that they were made at the beginning of creation, they were nevertheless made by God. For some other things that are not written down are shown by how other things are to be understood. In the same way, the apostles must be understood to have been baptized, although no clear statement in the writings shows outright that they were. Some, however, want this to be understood from the testimony in which the Savior says, "He who has bathed does not need to wash." But as for the waters being made by God, we can be instructed to some extent by the testimony that says, "Let the waters be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear." For he would surely not have commanded the waters to be separated from the earth he had made unless he had made the waters too; nor would he afterwards, in the order of creation, have ordered something to be set apart that he had not created before. We infer this because Genesis made no explicit mention of their creation. But the psalm points to God as the author of this creature more plainly when it says, "For the sea is his, and he made it."
What does it mean when it says, "And the Lord saw that they were very good"?
"Saw" means "approved."
What is the logic of the word [?] that it should be written: "She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man"?

The etymology, which does not come through here in Latin, is preserved in the Hebrew language, for man is called ish and woman ishshah. The recent translation is seen to have kept this beautifully when it says: "She shall be called virago, because she was taken from vir."
In what do we retain the likeness of God?
In the mind.
Where is paradise determined to be?

Many hold differing opinions on this matter. Some, however, determine that it is on earth, since an earthly being could not have lived anywhere but on earth; yet they maintain that it was made inaccessible to humankind by divine power.
What are we to take Eden to be in Genesis?
The most sacred place itself, toward the east of paradise.
What is to be understood about that tree of the knowledge of good and evil?

First of all, it must not be thought from this, as certain heretics interpret it, that God is the creator of evil things as well as of good. For in that tree, whatever it was, we must understand the command of God. In keeping the command lay the knowledge of good; in transgressing the command lay the knowledge of evil. So once the tree was tasted, that is, once the law of the command was violated, there came the knowledge of evil, because punishment followed upon the transgression of the command and the law.
How are we to take the fact that Scripture has told us that God walked in paradise?

By the word "walking" it makes plain the presence of God in that place. For it is the custom of Scripture to show divine movements and dispositions through human expressions, so that they may be clearer to human understanding. Thus when it speaks of the arm of God, it signifies his might and power; when it speaks of his ears, it means that he hears all things without fail; when of his eyes, that he sees all things without exception; when of his soul, that he lives forever and always, or that all things are given life by him as their author.
Since God made all things good, and there is nothing that was not made by him, where does evil come from?

From the privation of good, when what a good Creator brought forth for good is corrupted into evil by those who use it badly. In the very substance of a creature, however, there is nothing that can rightly be called evil. Further, the things thought to be evil — serpents, for instance, and the other kinds of beasts — become harmful through a mismatch between natures. The venom that brings death to a human being is life to the serpent. Indeed, if man had remained forever immortal, he would not fear to suffer harm from venom. In the same way some creatures live in water which die when put on land, and conversely others live on land which perish when plunged into water.
Since the substance of all creation came forth from God as its author, I ask what we should think about darkness.

Some argue on this point as follows: we speak of silence where there is no sound, yet we know that silence has no substance. In the same way, since there is no darkness where light is present, darkness is rightly reckoned to be the absence of light. Others, however, think this opinion hardly fits the testimony where it is written: "Yours is the day, and yours is the night."
Since there can be no ignorance in God, how is it that at the beginning of the book of Genesis the Lord himself says, "Adam, Adam, where are you?"

This is as much as to say: "Adam, where have you gone off to?" So this is not the voice of someone asking because he is uncertain, but of one questioning with a rebuke. Or again: this saying does not show God ignorant of the truth or unaware of where Adam was. Rather, it shows that everyone who sins, as if already straying by his errors and withdrawing from God's sight through his offense, becomes unworthy of God's knowing him.
What does it mean when it says, "Cursed is the ground in your works"?
Some think that "works" here are to be understood not so much as the cultivating and working of the field as sins.
How are we to understand the words, "And he dwelt in the land of Naid"?
Naid, or, as the Hebrew has it, Nod, means "unstable." So it is not the name of a land; rather, it declares that Cain was a wanderer and a fugitive, in accordance with God's punishment and sentence.
Since above it had designated both man and woman by their own names, why does it go on to add, "He made them male and female, and blessed them, and called their name Adam"?
Adam means "human being," and it is clear that by the name "human being" a woman can be called as much as a man.
Why is it that, on careful calculation, fourteen of Methuselah's years are found to extend beyond the flood, when we are told that only eight souls were in the ark?
There is an error in the numbers, since in the books of the Hebrews it reads in such a way that this number of fourteen years is completed before the time of the flood.
Since the Lord says, "Their days shall be a hundred and twenty years," how is it that afterwards the lifespans of Abraham and many others stretch beyond this length?

Because there this number of years had been assigned for doing penance rather than for human life: within the prescribed number of years they were to devote themselves to confession, so that they would not perish in the flood. Or, if one prefers to refer that number rather to human life — since even now no one is allowed to live more than a hundred and twenty years — then the saying "Their days shall be a hundred and twenty years" was pronounced not about those who came immediately after, but about later generations, for he did not say "let them be" but "they shall be."
"May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem": what is to be understood by this?

From Japheth, whose name in our language means "breadth," springs the multitude of the Gentiles; from Shem, the Hebrews. So what is signified is that, once Israel had been cast out, the knowledge of God and of the Scriptures would be claimed by our people. It should also be noted that the three sons of Noah occupied three parts of the earth after the flood: the descendants of Shem spread into Asia, or the East; those of Ham into Africa, or the South; and those of Japheth, along with part of Asia, into Europe and the West.
What does it mean when Genesis says, "And from that land went out Asshur, and built Nineveh and the city Rehoboth"?
It does not mean two cities, for Rehoboth means "streets." So the sense here is: he built Nineveh and the streets of the city.
How are we to answer those who object that Abraham took Sarah, his brother's daughter, as his wife?
We should reply that things which had not yet been forbidden by the Lord's law at that time were not thought unlawful.
Why was it that for the Jews a sign was placed on that more shameful part of the body — something we cannot even ask about without embarrassment?

The depth of such great questions, my Salonius, would indeed demand that we satisfy what has been put to us with an orderly and ample discussion, and give each question, as its merits deserve, the dignity of being dwelt upon. But what can we do? Since we must hurry on to so many things, the matters you have raised call for a bare and pared-down answer. So, as to what you now ask, recognize that nothing can be seen as shameful in the very creation of man, since God fashioned the whole man with the entire structure of his limbs. Further, it was not unfitting that that race should receive the sign on the part of the generative member through which the beginnings of that very race were brought forth. And indeed, according to the inner sense of understanding, this circumcision of a more hidden part of the body prefigured that a more hidden circumcision, that of the heart, ought to be applied.
It is written in Genesis, "God tested Abraham," as if the Lord did not know whether Abraham would be faithful to God unless he tested him with a trial that would make the matter plain.
God did not test Abraham to find out the truth because he did not know his faith; rather, he was tested so that, having been tested, he might be justified.

How can Jacob say, "I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved," when we read in the Gospel, "No one has ever seen God"? Or how is it written that Moses spoke with God face to face, as with a friend, and yet the same Moses says to the Lord, "Show me your glory"?

Because Jacob and Moses had not seen God in the very glory of his majesty, but through the form of a visible creature, subject to the divine power, which could appear to human eyes. But how could God be seen by a man still mortal in the substance of majesty in which he exists, when he himself says to Moses, "You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live"? In this way, then, both testimonies are true.
What does it mean when it says, "This is Anah, who found Iamin in the desert, while he was pasturing the asses of Zibeon his father"?

Iamin is rendered in Latin as "seas," that is, a gathering of waters, meaning that he discovered a pool — no doubt a hard thing to find in the desert. Iamin also indicates the asses that were born from wild asses through his arrangement. There are some who think that he was the first to discover the crossing of different animals with one another, so that mules, male and female, were born.
What is the birthright that Esau sold to his brother Jacob?

The first and greater share was owed to the firstborn, whether in honor or in the succession of inheritance, as Jacob himself says: "Reuben, my firstborn, first in gifts, greater in rule." And in the book of Deuteronomy it is written of the firstborn: "And he" — that is, the father — "shall give him a double portion of all that he has; for he is the first of his children, and the birthright is owed to him." That is also why Isaac had thought his blessing should go to Esau by right of the firstborn.
What should we answer those who think our fathers, the patriarchs, should be charged with incontinence because of their many wives?

First, that at that time it was not yet forbidden by law, and because it was the custom, it could not be a crime. Second, that those things were not disapproved by God at that time, by reason either of place or of time. Of place: just as in one house a master may order something to be done in one corner that he in no way allows to be done in another. Of time: because when the world was still young the command had been, "Increase and multiply," whereas now we are commanded that "those who have wives should be as though they had none." This is not because justice varies, but because times change; they cannot all run alike, and different things suit different times and different places. Finally, it must be that in these matters, by the Lord's will, a certain foretelling of things to come lay under the appearance of present deeds.
What does it mean when it says, "And behold, a vine before me, and behold, on the vine three stocks"?
By this mention of three stocks, three shoots or three runners are indicated.
ON EXODUS.

God tells Abraham that the children of Israel would return from the land of Egypt in the fourth generation. How then does Moses later write, "And in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt"?

If you trace the genealogy through the tribe of Levi, you will count four generations by the succession of sons; if you go through the line of the tribe of Judah, you will find five successive generations. In the Hebrew, however, as the version of Aquila, that most painstaking translator, shows, it does not read "they went up in the fifth generation" but "the children of Israel went up armed from the land of Egypt."
In the Scriptures we often read, "And the Lord said." How is this "saying" of the Lord to be understood?

The Lord is written to "say" or "speak" when he makes the sound of distinct words reach the ears of the saints, though often it is not heard by others; or when God speaks through the form of some body he has taken on; or when someone is instructed by the warning of a vision in the night; or, certainly, when the Lord breathes into the hearts of the saints the things he wants done, so that they may be done, according to the verse: "I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me."
The Lord says to Moses, "You shall see my back." What is to be understood here?
That he would see, either in the spirit or in his descendants, the latter works of God, which were to be revealed in Christ in the last times.
What should we reply to those who ask why God gave the law through Moses to only one nation, and that only after a great age of the world had already passed?

That the law was not given to the Jews alone, since it is inborn in all nations by the constitution of the natural law. The apostle confirms this when he says: "For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written on their hearts." And so the Lord was not late in gathering the law of innocence into ten words, since its origin had already been planted in human hearts beforehand. Nor was he slow to inscribe it again on tablets of stone, since he had already engraved it on the pages of the heart. For before this law of Moses, nature had its own law, by which it was readily possible to acknowledge God as the author of the world and of life, and so to love him, and to keep justice and love toward one's neighbor; on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. So they already knew this too: "Whatever you want people to do to you, do to them as well; for this is the law and the prophets." And to prove this also by examples: before this written law, through that law of nature, Abel is recognized as righteous, Enoch is taken up, Noah is chosen, and Abraham is called the father of the nations. For this reason the law of nature that went before, through which many proved themselves acceptable to God, shows that this law of Moses was not given too late.
What is that finger of God by which the two tablets of the law are said to have been inscribed?
The finger of God is to be understood here as the Spirit of God.
ON LEVITICUS.
Why is honey forbidden to be offered in the sacrifices?

Because, according to the inner sense, those who have gone slack through the allurements of delights or the sweetness of pleasures cannot share in the mysteries of God. That is also why the Lord's Passover is commanded to be eaten with bitterness: the strictness of truth is always stern. We ought, then, always to offer God saving sacrifices without any of the harmful honey of flattery and pleasure, and to say, "Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?" On the other hand, salt is commanded to be mixed into all the sacrifices — so that everything we offer for the honor and worship of Christ may always receive the salt of reason and discernment.
Of the things the people offered, what properly belonged to the use of the priests, and what to that of the Levites?
The firstfruits of the crops and of other things were assigned to the priests, and the tithes to the Levites; yet a tenth of those tithes was owed to the priests.
All the things God created are very good; how then are some animals called unclean in the law?

To say nothing of the other things that could be said on this point, they were called unclean with respect to eating, not to creation. For it is known that their use as food was forbidden by divine law for the sake of certain figures.
Since clean and unclean animals were distinguished by the divine law given through Moses, how is it that even before the flood some of the animals to be taken into the ark are called unclean?

Moses, inspired by the Holy Spirit, is the writer and composer of the Pentateuch. Since in Leviticus he was to set out the distinction between clean and unclean animals, he also called the same animals unclean in Genesis, because the same author wrote both books.
What in the Old Testament should we leave behind, and what should we observe?

We should observe the commandments that concern the correction of life and morals, but leave behind the ceremonies and rites of sacrifice, which at that time held up figures and a shadow of things to come.

What shall we answer those who object, asking why God rejected the old sacrifices and took delight in new ones? For they maintain that nothing is corrected unless it is thought not to have been done rightly.

This is a wide question, but as necessity requires we will answer briefly: God cannot be considered changeable because these things were changed to suit the times. For the year too varies with its seasons, and the span of life with its ages. Nor does the plan of divine providence that established these things change on that account; nor, if a farmer orders one thing in summer and another in winter in working his field, does the method of farming change. It is not the one who acts who seems unlike himself, but the time in which he acts. God, then, commands what is suited to each particular time. So too here he gave commands about sacrifices not for his own delight but, like everything else, for human benefit. And so he is the true Lord, because he has no need of our goods. But lest this very change of sacraments be thought something new and suddenly adopted, it had long ago been foretold by prophetic and divine voices, where it is said: "I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks." Finally, to conclude briefly why God willed different sacrifices to be offered to him: it was fitting that Christ be foretold by some sacraments when he was yet to come, and proclaimed by others once he had come.
ON NUMBERS.
Balaam was a Gentile. Why, then, does the trustworthy account of sacred history show that he prophesied?

So that the truth might become known in many ways, being proclaimed everywhere and announced even through unbelievers, and so that this prophecy from a Gentile might be a sign to the Gentiles who would come to believe. For Elihu, too, in the book of Job, undoubtedly foretold many things to come, and Caiaphas prophesied about our Lord and Saviour in the Gospel.
ON DEUTERONOMY
Deuteronomy records that only seventy souls entered Egypt with Jacob. How, then, is it later said in the Acts of the Apostles that seventy-five souls went into Egypt?

It is certain that at the time Jacob entered Egypt there were only seventy souls, counting Joseph and his sons Ephraim and Manasseh. But where the number seventy-five is given, the writer thought it right to count in advance, so to speak, the sons and grandsons of Ephraim and Manasseh as well, who the account of divine Scripture shows were born later in Egypt.
What answer should be given to the Jews when they bring up the text, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree"?

That the one who hangs on a tree is cursed, but the guilty one, not the innocent. The curse that is the penalty for sin cannot fall on innocence. If Mordecai had been hanged on the gallows prepared for him, and the sentence of the king's cruelty had been carried out, would they now judge him worthy of this curse? Or are the Maccabees, and others whom Scripture records as most shamefully afflicted with a similar death, counted as accursed among them? Therefore our Saviour, who was to redeem humanity from death, did not shrink from the cross, just as he did not shrink from death. So let them not cavil over the lesser things, when we glory in the Lord's endurance even in the greater. Nor is it surprising that he should be said to have undergone the gibbet, when we also confess that he descended into hell: though he had no sin of his own, he nevertheless took on the death that comes from the curse of sin. And that is why he hung on a tree: so that, hung on a tree, he might free us from the sin of perdition that had been committed at a tree.
ON JOB
How should we understand what Scripture mentions in Job, "the gold of Ophir"?

Ophir is a region stretching toward India, and so the phrase refers to the gold of that region. Others maintain that the gold of Uphaz is very precious, the gold that in Latin is called obryzum, refined gold.
What is meant by the fact that we read there, after the manner of secular authors, of the Pleiades, Orion, and Arcturus?

Not that these stars are known by these names among the Hebrews. Rather, so that what these constellations signify might be clearer to us, the translator chose to call them by the names that Gentile usage had given them. It should also be noted as a general rule that even the apostles and apostolic men, writing in their letters to the peoples, sometimes make use of testimonies that seemed to be widely known among those peoples.
In the same book, what is meant by what is written about that dragon: "If all the ships came together, they could not bear the skin of his tail"?

By ships he means the churches, which, harassed by temptations and tribulations, will barely endure the Antichrist at the end of the world. And he rightly calls the Antichrist the tail of that dragon, the devil, since from him the final persecution will come.
ON KINGS
Why does the Lord later reject Saul as king, when he had earlier thought fit to choose him for the kingship?

Because God brings forth his just and incorruptible judgment from equity, not from foreknowledge: he chose a man when he deserved it, and rejects him when he becomes unworthy of being chosen. Otherwise it would in no way seem consistent with his most holy truth and justice for his displeasure to come before the sin.
How should we understand the fact that Scripture often says the Lord repents, as also with Saul, when he says, "I repent that I made Saul king"?

The Lord's repentance means a change in what he has established, which follows upon changing circumstances or in accordance with the right ordering of things. For divine dispositions must be described in terms drawn from the human mind, so that they may become clearer to those who hear.
We read that an evil spirit of the Lord was choking Saul. How can it be "of the Lord" if it is evil?

Because everything brought into being by the Lord as its author is subject to divine power. So even the devil himself belonged to the Lord: not as he is now, but as he was once created good by the Lord, and as he is always subject to God under the dominion of the Almighty.
Why is it that the Lord punishes some things here, but not everything?
He punishes some things so that it may be understood that he takes care of human affairs; he does not punish everything so that all may recognize that a terrible judgment is still to come.
How was the woman with a spirit of divination able to call up the shade of Samuel?

Either the devil showed the onlookers a false shade, or, if it was real, we must believe that he was allowed only as much as the Lord permitted. Nor is it surprising that such things are permitted to the devil for certain hidden and secret reasons, or to bring trials to light, since he even set the Saviour on the pinnacle of the temple, and asked for Job to be tempted and was granted it.
Since there is no such thing as fate [?], how are fifteen years added to Hezekiah as he prays, as though to a predetermined span of life?

Because Hezekiah was pressed to his end not by a decree of fate but by God's summons and judgment; and the years of his life had not been fixed beforehand in such a way that they could not be understood to have been added through his supplication.
ON THE PROPHETS
How should we understand what the prophet Micah says: "Behold, the Lord comes out of his holy place, and comes down, and treads upon the high places of the earth"?

The Lord is said to come down when he is shown by clear signs of his most gracious kindness to care for human frailty. In the same way, the angels ascending and descending on Jacob's ladder signify the visiting of earthly things, not the fall of angels coming down. So too men who are loftier in righteousness are said to come down when, moved by holy charity, they stoop to those below them.
ON ISAIAH

What are we to understand in the song of the prophet Isaiah when he says: "I will sing to my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard: my beloved had a vineyard on a horn, the son of oil"?

Some think this song is sung by the Holy Spirit, others by the prophet, who was likewise not without the Holy Spirit. He sings it as a lament for his vineyard, which is the house of Israel. The beloved is Jesus Christ, for it was to him that it was said, "You are my beloved Son." He also calls him kinsman, because he was born of the same stock. This vineyard, then, was planted for him on a horn, that is, on a height and in strength; and he who is beloved is also the son of oil, because he was anointed, which is why he is called Christ, or because he has shone upon the whole world like a brilliant light. In this song he calls justice the grape and iniquity the thorns.

In Isaiah's vision, when he saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, how are we to understand what he says: "Seraphim stood above it; one had six wings and the other six wings. With two he covered his face, with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew; and one called to another and said, Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts"?

John the Evangelist testifies that in this vision it was the Lord Jesus Christ whom Isaiah saw, saying, "Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him." The first question here, then, is how the seraphim standing around the Lord's throne can be said to fly at the same time. The prophet expresses this well in mystical language, for to stand before God is the same as to fly and to rise on high; [?] he who hastens to appear before the divine gaze. As for the seraphim being shown covering the face with their wings, this is because neither any human being nor any creature can behold the light of the divine majesty as it is. They veil the face and the feet, then, because what was before the world and what will be after the world are hidden from us. The wings of the seraphim also signify the swiftness of their divine service; and each has six because we behold in the world only what was made in six days. And when they call to one another and say, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts," they show the one Godhead in the mystery of the Trinity.

What do we answer those who say to us: "What did the Jews do wrong, if they could not believe? For the word of the prophet Isaiah had to be fulfilled, which says: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn, and I heal them"?

The prophet foretold this because God foreknew that it would happen. God, whom sin cannot please, cannot compel anyone to sin. In these matters, then, we must understand not divine predestination but foreknowledge. Of this it is written in the Gospel: "Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart," and so on. "They could not believe" is said in the same way that we too are often said to be unable to do something because we are unwilling. And of Pharaoh it is written: "For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you." He did not say, "For this I made you, that you should be such a man," but, "For this I chose and raised you up, since you had already made yourself such a man." So here too their eyes are said to have been blinded and their heart hardened because they had already made themselves deserving of this blindness. The Lord blinds and hardens the sinner by abandoning him and not helping him. But if this explanation of a most profound question does not satisfy someone, let him tremble with me and say, "The judgments of the Lord are a great deep," for God's judgments are always just, but often hidden.
What does it mean when it is written: "He has set a mitre on me like a bridegroom, and adorned me with ornaments like a bride"? How can the same one be bridegroom and bride?

He has passed from the head to the body. For the head is Christ and the body is the Church, yet both are known to be in Christ. This rule should be noted and kept in mind, for it occurs frequently in the prophets and causes obscurity for those who do not know it: the course of prophecy turns either from the head to the body or from the body to the head.
"Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool." How can this be understood, since we certainly believe that God is incorporeal?
Following our ordinary way of speaking, it seems to describe the bearing of one who reigns, so that God may be understood either to dwell in the heavens or to have earthly things beneath him.
ON EZEKIEL

Why is it written: "In that great day of tribulation no one will be delivered except Noah, Daniel and Job," when, at the time the prophet Ezekiel said this, perhaps only Daniel was alive in the body, while the other two were already sleeping in peace, released from the bonds of the flesh?

These three saints seem to signify three kinds of people who are promised deliverance from danger on that day of tribulation. In Noah the governors of the Church are prefigured; in Daniel, the saints who pursue continence; in Job, married people who love righteousness.
What is meant by what the prophet says: "I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh"?
By describing it as stone he shows a hard and disobedient heart; by calling it flesh he shows a heart that is soft and teachable, able to receive the compunction instilled in it.
ON CHRONICLES
What is meant by what is written in Chronicles: "who lived in Jerusalem in the second"?
"In the second" means in the second part. For Hezekiah built a second wall around Jerusalem, and his son Manasseh a third; so the woman spoken of here lived in the second part of the city.
Where are we to believe the ark of the Lord, which held the two tablets of the covenant, was taken?
We read in Chronicles that Josiah king of Judah, when he was keeping the Passover to the Lord in Jerusalem, spoke to the Levites as follows: "Put the ark in the sanctuary of the temple which Solomon

the son of David, king of Israel, built; for you shall carry it no longer." Some take this passage to mean that Josiah, foreseeing what was to come [?], took care to have the ark of the Lord hidden at that time, though in what place is uncertain.

What is the difference between a burnt offering and a sacrificial victim? The priests ate part of the victim, whereas the burnt offering was a whole and complete victim, because the entire animal was given to the fire in the offering of the sacrifice. There were also the victims called peace offerings, which the people used to eat.
ON THE BOOK OF PSALMS

The first psalm, in its opening verses, distinguishes the ungodly, the sinner and the heretic. What, then, is meant by the conclusion at the very end of the psalm, where it says, "Therefore the ungodly shall not rise again in the judgment"?

The beginning of this psalm concerns the distinction of merit, and the end the distinction of judgment. In it he shows that every human being will without doubt rise again: the righteous to judge, the sinner to be judged, the ungodly to be punished. For the ungodly will not be judged then, having already been judged, as it is written: "But he who does not believe is judged already."
Since passion has no place in God, why does Scripture often speak of God's anger and fury?

It is the custom of Scripture to use anger for vengeance. It is anger from the human point of view, punishment from God's, and fury as it feels to the one who suffers it, not as it is in the justice of the one who judges. The same applies to what is said in the prophet: "The Lord, who creates evil." These things are evil, then, as felt by the one who endures them, not in the equity of the one who decrees them.
What is meant by the phrase often written in the titles of the psalms, "Unto the end, a psalm of David"?

That the psalms look to the promise of good things at the end of the world; or that what the Jews believed at the beginning they could obtain, we attain in Christ, whom we shall confess to have come at the end.
How should we understand what is written: "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried in the fire, proved, purified of earth seven times"?
The words of the Lord are called pure because they are corrupted by no falsehood, and, like silver tried in a sevenfold fire, they are purified by the fire of the Spirit.
"I will not gather their assemblies of bloods," he says. "Of blood" would certainly have sounded more like Latin, so why is "of bloods" written, against the rules of Latin?
In the Greek one reads haimatōn, which signifies blood in the plural; and the translator, faithful to this peculiarity, rendered it into Latin in the plural as well.
Since it is written in a psalm, "You will not let your holy one see corruption," how is it written again in another psalm, "What profit is there in my blood, while I go down to corruption?"

The Saviour declares through the prophet's voice that he goes down into corruption when he is pierced by the nails driven into him. On the other hand, the Lord did not let his holy one see corruption, because Christ forestalled the corruption of the flesh by his swift resurrection.
What does the prophet mean when he says of his enemies, "They have shut up their fat"?

The fat of the ungodly is shut up when, grown fat in mind and thick with iniquity, they turn away from righteousness or from God's commandments. That is why he says elsewhere: "Their iniquity shall come forth from their fat." Manna, on the other hand, that is, the heavenly food, is fine, and suited to nourish those who are strong in fineness of understanding.
What are we to think of what is written: "Their belly is filled with your hidden things; they are filled with swine's flesh, and have left what remained to their little ones"?

Above he asked that the Jews be separated from the few, that is, from the righteous, for "many are called, but few are chosen." Now he says that these same people, first instructed in the hidden things of the divine law, and afterwards glutted with their swine's flesh, that is, with the filth of their doctrines, have handed on that same impiety to their descendants as well, by denying Christ.
How should we understand: "Day pours forth speech to day, and night shows knowledge to night"?

Day pours forth speech to day when the apostles proclaim the Saviour to believers. Night shows knowledge to night when Judas pours the teaching of perverse understanding into the Jews. Or else, day pours forth speech to day and night shows knowledge to night when, every day and night, the word and knowledge are spread through the preaching of the faithful.
"Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me." What distinction is to be understood here?
The rod signifies correction, the staff comfort.
Since animals are not without perception, how does the psalm say, "Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding"?
Because animals have perception, but human beings have understanding.
Since God does not care for beasts of burden, as he does not care for oxen, how does the psalm say, "And you will save beasts, O Lord"?
He calls those capable of reason human beings, and those without reason beasts. He affirms that the former will be saved through their present way of life, the latter through their future conversion.
How should we take what is written: "Spare me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and am no more"?

The meaning here is made clear by the verses before. For he had said above: "For I am a stranger with you, and a sojourner, like all my fathers. Spare me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and am no more"; and what he said earlier, "sojourner," is to be understood. Otherwise it is clear that he will exist, since by calling himself a sojourner above he declares that he has a homeland where he is to be.
What is meant by what we read in the psalm: "At the head of the book it is written of me"?

This is said in the person of the Saviour, of whom it is written, "In the beginning God created heaven and earth," that is, in the Son; or else that other text, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
"Deep calls to deep," he says, "at the voice of your cataracts." How should this be understood?

The depth of the divine Scriptures is rightly called a deep. And so deep calls to deep at the voice of the cataracts when the Old Testament proclaims the New, or the New Testament calls the Old to bear witness in the voices of the prophets.
What are we to understand from what is written: "Instead of your fathers, sons are born to you"?
That is, in the succession of the ages the apostles have been given in place of the prophets.
"A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem." What are we to think of this passage?
That what Moses did not redeem, Christ redeemed.
How should we take what David cries out to the Lord, saying, "Against you only have I sinned"?

Sin is committed against God alone, because he alone is without sin. So, being justified, he prevails even when he is judged: that is, either Christ in his passion, or according to what the Lord says in the prophet, "Come, and let us be judged together, says the Lord."
"Men of blood and deceit," he says, "shall not live out half their days." What should we think here?

Those who are carried off by an untimely death do not live out half their days. In this sense we can also understand the verse, "Do not snatch me away in the midst of my days." And another interpretation: those who do not give even part of their life to making satisfaction to God do not live out half their days.
What is the inner meaning of what is written: "Before your thorns produce the bramble"?
That is, before your sins come to their full measure.
How does the righteous man wash his hands in the blood of the sinner?
When vengeance is dealt out on the wicked without the saints seeking it; and, after the sins and end of the sinners, the life and works of the righteous shine more brightly.
How should we take what we read in the psalm: "Do not have mercy on any who work iniquity"?

This is said not so much in the spirit of one who curses as of one who desires the correction and amendment of sinners: that is, that they may rather be corrected in this present life and not abuse God's patience until they meet the bitterness of punishment to come.
"God has spoken once; these two things I have heard." What is to be understood here?

"Once" here refers not to number but to firmness. And what are those two things that belong to the Lord? Both that he can do all things and that he wills to have mercy. Another interpretation: "God has spoken once," that is, in the law; for in the Gospel he does not command anything different, for he says, "I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it."
What is meant by what is written: "We went through fire and water, and you brought us into a place of refreshment"?

By fire and water he signifies persecutions and martyrdom. Some think that here water should be understood as baptism, and fire as the Holy Spirit, who, poured in, burns up sins like fire; hence it is written, "The Lord your God is a consuming fire."
What does the passage mean: "Make a way for him who rises above the setting; the Lord is his name"?
Prepare the way of good deeds for him who has passed beyond the setting by conquering death.
"You will set apart a willing rain, O God, for your inheritance, and it was weakened, but you have perfected it; your creatures shall dwell in it." What is the meaning of this passage?

The rain here is to be understood literally as the manna, and in the anagogical sense as the commandments. These commandments, or the law, though they seem to have been weakened by the transgressions of the Jews, are nevertheless shown to have been fulfilled by the grace of the Gospel, in which the creatures, that is, the Gentiles, now dwell and stand firm.
What understanding is there in what we read: "If you sleep among the lots, the wings of the dove are covered with silver, and the hinder parts of her back with the sheen of gold"?

In this passage the prophet prays for the apostles, that they may persevere, believing in the two testaments, until their passing. In the dove the Holy Spirit is shown; in the hinder parts, a more hidden understanding; in the silver, the shining history of the Scriptures; in the gold, the inner and more precious meaning.

"The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back into the depths of the sea, that your foot may be dipped in blood, and the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him." What sense do we follow here?

In Latin, Bashan means "confusion." So the Lord turns us back from the confusion that lies in his cross. On that cross he dipped his foot in blood, while the Jews, urged on by his enemies, that is, by the demons, cried out for him to be crucified. Yet all of this came from the Saviour himself, since he endured all these things of his own will.
Whom are we to take as those princes of Zebulun or princes of Naphtali?
The apostles Peter and Andrew, who were called from those same tribes, just as above, under the name of Benjamin, the apostle Paul is to be understood.
What is meant by the words: "They set up their standards as standards, and did not know, as at the way out above the summit"?
It means that the Babylonians, made arrogant by victory, displayed their standards in the temple of God, just as standards are usually set up as trophies over arches and the entrances of gates.
What is meant by the words: "But God our king before the ages has worked salvation in the midst of the earth"?

He means Judea, where Christ set the world free through the cross; some think it should be called the navel of the earth. Another interpretation: "He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth," that is, in the virgin's womb.
What is meant by what we read: "For in the hand of the Lord there is a cup full of unmixed wine, mixed; and he has poured from this into that; yet its dregs have not been emptied"?

The Lord's cup is mixed with mercy and judgment. It is poured from one into the other when divine severity passes from mercy to judgment. Its dregs, however, are not emptied, because the last judgment is still held in reserve.
What is the meaning of the words: "And the remainder of thoughts shall keep a feast day for you"?
This beautifully shows that God delights in purity of mind as in a kind of festival.
"The voice of your thunder," it says, "in the wheel." How should this be understood?
By "wheel" here he means the globe of the earth itself, because the thunder carries its roar around within the wheel of that globe.
How are we to understand the words: "And he struck his enemies in the hinder parts"?

In the literal sense, this recalls the sores with which the Philistines were struck in their hinder parts. In the inner sense, the enemies of God are struck in the hinder parts when the Lord punishes them at the last judgment.
Whom does he mean when he says: "The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed on it"?
Some say that by the boar he means Vespasian, who devastated the Jews in war, and by the solitary wild beast Titus, Vespasian's son, who destroyed Jerusalem by siege.
We read in a psalm: "Israel, if you will listen to me, there shall be no new god in you." How are we to take this?

He declares that idols, or the Antichrist, are to be rejected. Christ, however, was not a new god, even though in our times he shone upon the world through the flesh. For in the beginning God the Word was with God; he himself created man in the likeness of God, and at various times and seasons he always appeared to Abraham and to our fathers.
How are we to take what the psalm says: "God has stood in the assembly of gods"?

That is, in the congregation of the saints. Our Lord has granted his saints a share in his name, just as he has granted them a share in his kingdom. That is why he says to Moses: "I have made you a god to Pharaoh." So they are addressed by the name of God because they are also called sons of God. Given the ineffable generosity of the divine kindness, it is no wonder that he willed man to be called god, since God was called man.
How should we understand this: "Justice and peace have kissed each other"?
Is it not that the law and grace have been joined together through the mediator, our Lord Jesus Christ, who made the two one?
How are we to take what we read: "The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob"?
It means that the Lord has preferred the fortifications of the Church to the shadowy shelters of the synagogue.
"Mother Zion shall say: a man, and a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her." What interpretation do we follow here?

Some hold that Mother Zion signifies Mary, in whom Christ was born as man, he who was also the creator of his own mother. It should be known, however, that it is better, and more faithful to the Hebrew, to read: "Shall a man say to Zion, 'A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her'?" The sense here is: which of men could announce this? It is like the words: "Or to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" So this is what he is saying: no man could declare that Zion would be saved in a man who would be born in her. And that man himself is the Most High who founded her. Note also that the Son is called the Most High.
What are we to understand where it is written: "I have become like a man without help, free among the dead"?
Christ was certainly free among the dead, because he appeared among sinners without sin.
What is that land of forgetfulness of which it is said: "Shall your wonders be known in the darkness, and your justice in the land of forgetfulness"?

The flesh of the wicked, abandoned by the Lord, is quite rightly called the land of forgetfulness. Another interpretation: the land of forgetfulness can also be taken in the sense of the words: "For in death there is no one who remembers you; and in hell who will confess to you?"
How is the eagle's youth renewed, as we read: "Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's"?

Eagles are said to lose their feathers through extreme old age; they are then carried back to the nest and fed by their own young, who in turn take care of them, until they shake off the torpor of old age and recover their feathers and with them the power of flight. In the anagogical sense, however, our youth is renewed either by baptism or by the resurrection.
"The deep," it says, "like a cloak is his clothing." What interpretation do we follow here?

Many wrongly think that the deep is here called God's clothing. Rather, the order of the preceding verses itself makes clear that it is called the clothing of the earth, because the earth itself is surrounded or encompassed by the deep and veiled as if by a cloak.
How do waters stand above the mountains, since it is written: "The waters shall stand above the mountains"?
Clearly, either when clouds full of water hang over the mountains, or when the waves at sea are raised up like mountains.
How should we understand what we read: "This dragon, which you formed to be mocked by them"?

This dragon is the devil, but as he was formed by the Lord before he passed, at the prompting of his own wilful wickedness, into the name of devil. The prophet Isaiah describes him as being mocked by little children.
How are we to understand what is written: "The iron passed through his soul"?

Christ is very plainly signified here, because by rising again he overcame the pain and torment of the nails that fastened him. The iron here can also be understood as the tribulation of hard necessity, since he said "soul"; yet in the Scriptures "soul" is sometimes also used for the present life, as in the Gospel: "Is not the soul more than food?"

What is the difference between a psalm and a song? A psalm is named from the psaltery, whereas a song is produced by the voice. Also, a song stands for knowledge and a psalm for action. So the psalm relates to the active life, that is, to practice, and the song to the contemplative life, that is, to theory.
"The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent." How does the Lord swear?
For the Lord to swear is for him to promise unchangeably. So this figure of speech is rightly used, because his promise has the firmness of an oath.
What is meant by what is written: "He drank from the torrent on the way; therefore he lifted up his head"?

These words are to be referred to the person of Christ: he drank from the torrent, that is, the passion, on the way, that is, in this world. Therefore God, lifting up his head, gave him the name that is above every name.
Why are those fifteen psalms headed "A Song of Steps"?

Formerly, as history shows, one went up into the temple by fifteen steps. So these fifteen psalms are marked with the title "Song of Steps," because they lead us by a series of advances up to the heights of spiritual things.
"Sharp arrows of the mighty," it says, "with desolating coals." What is the meaning of this verse?

The mighty arrows are the words of the Lord, which pierce our hearts with his love. The desolating coals are those that lay waste our sins, like the coal of the prophet Isaiah, which was brought to his lips to purge the faults he had contracted either by speaking or by keeping silent out of fear.
What is meant by the words: "Behold, he who keeps Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep"?

In the Scriptures the Lord is sometimes said to sleep when it is really faith that sleeps in us and leaves the slumbering man unbelieving. But he cannot fail those who seek him, and he does not know how to sleep for those who keep watch.

We read in a psalm about Jerusalem: "Whose sharing is in the same." What interpretation shall we follow here? That different parts make up one city, or that different members form the one body of the Lord.
How should we understand the place where it is written: "Perhaps our soul would have passed through an immeasurable water"?

In place of "perhaps," the Greek has [?], which we render more clearly in Latin as "do you think?" So the sense is: Do you think our soul would have passed through the immeasurable water if the Lord had not been with us?

What is meant by the words: "Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the south wind"? This is the voice of a soul rejoicing as it returns from the chains of vice to freedom and conversion. It asks to be released from the captivity of sin by the breath of divine mercy, just as torrents bound by ice are released by the warmth of the south wind.
How are we to understand this: "Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward is the fruit of the womb. Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those shaken out"?

The prophet shows that he is speaking there of future things, since after that sitting he declares the time of rising: that is, after he has given sleep to his beloved, he shows what that resurrection of the saints will be, when he says: "Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward is the fruit of the womb." So the Lord's inheritance lies in sons, which he has obtained as the reward of the fruit of the womb. For the Saviour is the fruit of the womb, and his reward is that the nations, whom he begets as sons through faith, should be his inheritance. The apostles are rightly called arrows, for they ranged over the world as if in flight and pierced the hearts of unbelievers with their teaching. The prophet very aptly calls them sons of those shaken out, that is, of the prophets. For when the prophets are shaken out in their prophecy, what else is revealed in them but the apostles, found there? So, since the apostles were begotten from the prophets when these were shaken out, they are rightly called sons of those shaken out.
What is meant by what we read: "As a child weaned from its mother, so will you reward my soul"?

Our soul is weaned when its understanding is raised from the infancy of ignorance to the solid food of a perfected life. So he had said above: "If I did not think humbly," that is, if I did not think lowly and earthly thoughts, "but lifted up my soul," that is, if I strove toward heavenly things in mind, then let this be my reward: that my soul may attain the perfection of understanding.
"Blessed," it says, "is he who repays you what you have dealt to us." Who is to be understood here?

This psalm can be understood both of the captivity of the Jews, when they were led into Babylon, and of sinners who are expelled from the Church and handed over to confusion. Here, then, according to history, as some think, King Cyrus is meant, who repaid this retribution when he overthrew Babylon and raged there with total slaughter, even down to its little ones. But in the inner sense, he repays Babylon in kind who leads captive the soul that had formerly been held captive by the law of sin, and dashes the first beginnings of vices against the rock, which is Christ.
The Scriptures often say: "I confess to you, O Lord." How is this to be understood?
Confession does not always seem to mean penitence, for "I will confess" is sometimes used for "I will praise," or "I will give thanks," or "I will glorify the Lord."
"Your eyes," it says, "have seen my unfinished state, and in your book all shall be written." What is the meaning here?

God's eyes see our unfinished state because God knows a man even before he is formed. Another interpretation: God's eyes see our unfinished state because he looks into our thoughts even before they are completed. All are written in his book because no human being is born without his will, or because all our wishes are fully recorded before him. Then follows: "By day they shall be filled, and no one in them." By day, that is, they will be filled by Christ, and apart from Christ no one will be in them, because those who are full of God cannot receive what is not of God.
Who are the young ravens of whom it is written: "And to the young ravens that call upon him"?
It means faithful children born of unbelieving parents.
What is indicated by what we read: "Who can stand before the face of his cold?"
These words show the chill of temptations.
Why are those swords of the saints called two-edged, of which it is written: "And two-edged swords in their hands"?

The swords are called two-edged because in judgment they can punish both body and soul together. Another interpretation: because they punish both with the torment of present penalty and with the fear of future penalty. Hence also what is sung in the same psalm: a new song to the Lord, because those who are thought to be the refuse of the world will judge nations and kings.
ON THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON.
"Let the stag of friendship and the foal of graces converse with you." What interpretation shall we follow here?

Some think that the stag of friendship here should be taken as Christ, the teacher of all love and charity, and the foal of graces as the Holy Spirit, the distributor of all graces, that is, of the charisms. So we are admonished by this always to seek the comfort of Christ and of the Holy Spirit.
What is meant by the words: "Seven times the righteous man shall fall and rise again"?

Clearly, when he slips in speech or in thought, or else when he offends within the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. Some maintain that "seven times" is said here because of the seven days through which the course of human life revolves, since the course of life itself cannot be without sin.
ON ECCLESIASTES.
What is meant by what we read in Ecclesiastes: "And the almond tree shall blossom, and the locust shall grow fat, and the caper shall be scattered, because man shall go to the house of his eternity"?

They teach that these words signify the members of the human body: by the almond blossom he shows white hair, by the fattening of the locust the swelling of the feet, by the scattering of the caper the cooling of desire. When these things happen to an old man at the end of his life, he must then return to the earth, as to the house of his eternity. Yet this house of eternity is also well taken as that land of the future of which it is written: "I will please the Lord in the land of the living."
ON THE SONG OF SONGS.

What is meant by what is written of the Church: "I am dark and beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem"? If dark, how beautiful? Because before she is tried, the Church is divided in two according to the differences of those within her: in the saints she is beautiful, in sinners dark. Just so, Scripture sometimes calls Jerusalem the holy city and sometimes a sinner.

What does the word "cousin" (fratruelis) mean in the Song of Songs? The Church, in whose name these words are addressed there to the Saviour, calls Christ her cousin, since he is the son of the synagogue. And since our holy writers have at times chosen to regard the Church as the sister of the synagogue, Christ is called the Church's cousin as well as her bridegroom, following a certain way of speaking in Scripture.
ON THE MORE DIFFICULT QUESTIONS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT. ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

Why are the evangelists represented in the prophet by four different kinds of living creatures? Matthew has the form of a man, because he begins from the birth of a man, saying: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham." Mark is prefigured in the form of a lion, because like a lion he bursts out with a mighty voice: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord." Luke is announced in the calf, because he begins from the sacrifices, or from the priesthood, writing: "In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a certain priest named Zechariah." John is marked out by the eagle, because, soaring in spirit to the heights, he speaks as if from on high, saying: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
How are we to take the fact that the Lord Jesus Christ is called the son of David, when he was certainly not born of Joseph, who was descended from David's line?

At that time the Jews, according to the law, took in marriage their nearest kin. There can be no doubt that, for this reason, Mary too came from the same tribe and, like Joseph, was descended, or rather sprang, from David's line. The origin of Mary is indicated through Joseph's genealogy because it is the custom of the Scriptures to trace the line of descent through men rather than women. And since, as we read, Elizabeth was Mary's kinswoman, and Elizabeth is described as being of the daughters of Aaron, it is perfectly clear that in Christ, according to the flesh, both lineages came together: the succession of kings and that of priests.
The evangelist Matthew says that Joseph was begotten by Jacob. How then does Luke record that he was the son of Heli?

Because one was his father by nature, the other by law. For it was the custom among the Jews, based on the law, that a surviving brother should take his dead brother's wife to raise up offspring for him. Jacob and Heli, then, were brothers by the same mother; when the elder died, the younger took his wife in marriage according to the law. In recording them, Matthew traced Joseph's ancestry through the royal line, while Luke derived his descent through the priestly succession. Joseph's father by nature, however, was undoubtedly Jacob.
Why is Mary called Joseph's wife in the Gospel?
It is the custom of the Scriptures to call betrothed women wives as well.
What is meant by what we read: "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire"?

Because through the Holy Spirit our sins are burned away, or sanctification is granted, or the fervour of love is kindled for enduring sufferings. Or else because, once baptized in the Spirit, we will be tested by the divine judgment. There are some who say that the apostles were baptized with the Holy Spirit when fire appeared above them.

How are we to understand the body of that dove in which the Holy Spirit was seen plainly descending upon the Saviour? Did it already exist beforehand, or was it suddenly made for the occasion and appeared?

Certainly it was shown for the occasion. For, so that a visible sign of the Holy Spirit, who was invisible, might be displayed, we must believe that the body of that dove was indeed real, but made by divine power for the moment, that it appeared for an hour and then ceased to exist. Angels, when they present themselves to human eyes, are believed, in the opinion of some, to take on a body for the time being from this denser air, that is, the air near the earth. They are further thought to produce a voice in such a way that a blow struck against this air gives back the sound of words, as if from a palate.
The kingdom of heaven is promised to the righteous. How then is it also said: "For they shall possess the earth"?
Because a new heaven and a new earth are promised to the righteous in the future, so that then, like the angels, they may possess both together with God.

Since the Saviour says that Tyre and Sidon could have repented if the signs of divine power had appeared among them, why were the miracles that would have brought salvation to believers not done there?

Because the Lord and Saviour, by divine dispensation, had come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. And why had he come only to the sheep of the house of Israel? Because among all the other nations everywhere, Israel in a special way worshipped the one God and was once, so to speak, God's own peculiar people, on account of the merits of Abraham, the patriarchs, and David. To them Christ was specifically promised, and, descending from their line, he took from it the very flesh in which he appeared on earth. But since miracles were afterwards done among the Gentiles as well, this testimony can be understood in this way: where he says "I did not come," the word "first" is to be understood. So both the truth of the testimony and God's mercy, ready for all, shine out more clearly.
In the Gospel our Lord and Saviour says: "My yoke is easy and my burden is light." How then do we read in the psalm: "Because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways"?
It is indeed clear that all who wish to live godly lives in Christ suffer persecution. Yet for those who love God, things that are hard in present reality become light in the hope of things to come.
What are we to understand in the passage where it is written: "Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath"?

In the historical sense it should be understood this way: "that your flight may not be in winter," that is, that the hardship of flight may not be made worse by the harshness of the season; "that your flight may not be on the sabbath," that is, not on the very day on which you are accustomed to have rest and leisure. But in the higher sense, "that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath" can be taken thus: that the flight may not catch you either cold in sins or idle in good works.

In the same Matthew it is written: "But I say to you, I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father." What interpretation shall we follow here?
The kingdom of God, as the learned interpret it, is the Church, in which Christ daily drinks his own blood through his saints, as the head in his members.

Why is it said, "From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming on the clouds of heaven"? And in another place it is said that they will not see him coming on the clouds of heaven until the very last day: "All the tribes of the earth will mourn, and then they will see the Son of Man on the clouds of heaven."

Because the first passage announces the coming of the body, that is, of the Church, through the open display and splendour of signs, whereas the other is the coming of the head, that is, of Christ himself. In the first coming Christ comes through his members; in the second, in his own person.
ON MARK.
What is meant in the Gospel when it says, "For whoever has will be given more, and whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken from him"?

For example, if someone has faith but does not have love, he will lose even the faith that he perhaps seemed to have. The Jews are a case in point: because they did not understand Christ through the divine Scripture, they lost even the knowledge of God that they thought they held, and because they did not receive the Son, they do not have the Father either.
The evangelist Mark indicates that the Lord was crucified at the third hour of the day. How, then, does another evangelist record that it was the sixth hour when he was crucified?

Because one of them recorded in his writings roughly the hour at which he was actually crucified, while the other chose to record the time of an earlier hour, when sentence was passed on him as the Jews shouted against him. By anticipating events in his account, he presents him as crucified at the hour when he was ordered to be crucified. Yet in this very passion of his we must hold that the man who was assumed endured it by the will of that same Word, in such a way that the Word who was in the beginning with the Father remained unharmed and undefiled. What he had taken on for the sake of human weakness was therefore exposed to injury, while what divine eternity possessed remained incorruptible.
ON LUKE.
What is meant by what is written in Luke about the priest Zechariah, that he was of the division of Abijah?

The priests had been distributed into twenty-four divisions by lot for the service of the temple, so that each would perform the priestly office in the order of his turn. In this order Abijah held the eighth lot, and the priest Zechariah belonged to his division.
Who in the sacred Scriptures received their names before they were born?
In the New Testament, apart from the Saviour, we read only of John the Baptist. In the Old there are four: Isaac, Ishmael, Solomon and Josiah, whose names, it would seem, are older than they are.
How could John, still without senses in the womb, leap for joy in his mother's womb when the Lord's mother arrived?

Some think that it happened rather through the mother's own feeling or joy, so that her joy could leap even in her inmost womb. Or, if one prefers to refer it to John, it must certainly be counted among God's miracles, like the time when a donkey's voice broke out into the sound of speech.

In the same Gospel, what is the meaning of the passage that reads: "It happened on the second-first sabbath that he was passing through the grainfields, and his disciples were plucking ears of grain, rubbing them in their hands and eating them"?

Some think that the Lord's day is called this here because it seems to be second after the sabbath observed under the Law and is first in the celebration of the grace of the gospel. Someone may find this unsatisfactory and argue that the day was actually a sabbath, since it is written of it, "Why are you doing what is not lawful on the sabbath?" If so, perhaps that sabbath day itself can still be understood in this way: it is now second in our observance, though it was once first in Jewish observance. For the Lord's day is quite rightly reckoned the first day.
How is it that Luke says that the vision in which the Lord took three disciples with him and was glorified came eight days later, while the other evangelists say six days?

Luke, who writes that this vision was shown to the disciples eight days after the Lord had spoken with them, includes both the day on which the Lord spoke and the day on which Jesus appeared in glory. The others, who thought it right to state six days, counted only the whole days in between and left out the first and last days as being only partly full.

Again, in the same Gospel he says: "For from now on five in one house will be divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against his father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law." Why is it that, after he seems to have named five persons above, he goes on to list six?

The mother and the mother-in-law can be taken as the same woman, called by two names in relation to the daughter and the daughter-in-law. In that case the number of persons in what follows can also be seen to be five.

Several questions arise in the parable of Lazarus and the rich man. How can the rich man be in torment before the judgment? How can he speak of Lazarus's finger? Are there bodies in the underworld? And when he longs for water, was he feeling bodily thirst?

He says all these things in keeping with the feelings he once had because of the needs of the body. As for the sense of torment before the judgment, the place serves as a kind of prison, so that even before the judgment it is not without torments. Again, as to the fact that Abraham is seen [?] to be in the underworld, some think the reason is that all people, even the saints, are said to have gone down to the underworld before the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, though to a place of refreshment. Others think that the place where Abraham was is set above those regions of the underworld. That is why the Lord says of the rich man, "Lifting up his eyes while he was in torment, he saw Abraham far off." And Abraham's bosom, they think, signifies the rest of that region.
How should we take what we read: "The kingdom of God is within you"?

In each person either God or the devil reigns, depending on whether that person's deeds are good or evil, because whoever carries out someone's will by his actions must be regarded as subject to that one's rule. So if some people are righteous, God must be said to reign in them; if they are unrighteous, the devil does. Faith too can be called the kingdom of God, for by faith we travel to the kingdom, by it the righteous person lives, and through it Christ dwells in the hearts of his saints.
How is it that in Luke the Saviour says to the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise," when on that day, as man, his body was certainly in the earth and his soul in the underworld?

Perhaps paradise can be taken here as the place of rest that has been assigned, where the Saviour shows in the Gospel that Abraham is with Lazarus. Or else it must be understood that the Lord fulfilled this promise through the working of his divine power, since we must recognize that God is everywhere.
ON JOHN.
In the Gospel of John the Jews assert that the temple took forty-six years to build. How is it shown that forty-six years were spent?

It is well established that Solomon built the house of the Lord in only seven years, since Scripture says of it, "And he built it in seven years." The forty-six years, however, are assigned to the restoration of the temple, which took place in the days of Ezra, after the destruction of Jerusalem and the captivity of the Jews. This rebuilding of the temple dragged on for a long time because the surrounding nations hindered the work by constantly attacking it.

How did the Saviour take into heaven the man he had assumed, and how is heaven promised to the saints, when he says, "No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven"? And how was he in heaven when he was still on earth?

According to the flesh he was on earth; according to his divinity he was never absent from heaven. So the one who came down is also the one who went up, because although he assumed a man, man and God, that is, Christ, are one person. And since he is the head and the saints are the members, the members must follow where the head has gone before, so that the fullness of Christ's body may be in heaven.
How should we take what is written: "For God does not give the Spirit by measure"?

Some maintain that this must be understood as referring specifically to the Son. Because some human beings receive more and others less, they seem to receive the Spirit by measure, as the Apostle says: "We have gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: prophecy, in proportion to the measure of faith," and so on. But to Christ, his only-begotten Son, who also gives the Spirit, the Spirit was not given by measure, because the whole fullness of the Godhead is in him.
The Saviour says, "You go up to this day; I am not going up to this festival." How, then, is it written of him later, "But after his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the festival"?

The Truth cannot tell a lie, and so Jesus did nothing other than what he had declared he would do. The Feast of Tabernacles of the Jews takes in not one day but several days of celebration, just as the festival of Passover does. Since he had said, "I am not going up to this festival," he certainly did not go up to that particular feast day, as he had said beforehand. For the Gospel goes on: "Having said this, he"—that is, the Saviour—"remained in Galilee." We are meant to understand that it was during the same festival, but not on the same day as the one of which it is later written, "But after his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the festival." The feast day to which the Saviour declared he would not go up can also be understood figuratively, as teaching that the festival was to be transformed in him.
How should we understand the passage in which it is written of Jesus Christ our Saviour, "No one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come"?

This hour is not to be understood in the astrologers' sense, but rather as the hour in which he himself chose to be crucified and to suffer. His hour had not yet come because he had not yet finished everything, because he had not yet fulfilled all the work he had set out to do, the work for which he had come to visit humankind and the earth.
