How should we understand the Saviour's words: "When he tells a lie, he speaks from his own, for he is a liar and his father"?

Earlier the Lord had said to the Jews, "If God were your father, you would surely love me," and afterwards, "You are of your father the devil, and you want to carry out your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he tells a lie"—here we must understand "each one of you"—"he speaks from his own, for he is a liar and his father," that is, the devil. Some interpret it this way: "When he tells a lie," meaning the devil, "he speaks from his own, for he is a liar and his father"—that is, he is the father of the lie itself, since the lie seems to have originated from him. Just as God begot the Son, the Truth, so the devil begot a son, falsehood.
How should we take what is said: "Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day; he saw it and was glad"?

The prophets were called seers because, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, they saw things hidden from others, as though they knew the future in advance. Abraham was among them, and he saw Christ in the Spirit.
It is said in the Gospel, "We know that God does not listen to sinners." How, then, does the Saviour say in another place, "Everyone who asks receives"?

Some take it this way. The man who said that sinners are not heard, they say, had been blind, and having only just had his eyes anointed with salve, as it were, he could not yet see the full truth. It is certain, however, that the ear of divine mercy is open to those who knock. There is another way to understand how God does not listen to sinners: even if they are heard when they seek their own salvation, they are not heard when they ask for signs.
What does our Lord and Saviour mean when he says in the Gospel of John, "I came into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind"?

This is no small question, but since we must be brief we set out what the opinion of the learned holds on it. He came so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind. That is, those who admit that they do not see and look for a physician may see, while those who think they see and do not seek a physician may remain in their blindness. So he said that he had come for this judgment, to decide between the case of believers and that of unbelievers. "So that those who do not see may see" can be understood of the Gentiles, who were going to see through faith; and "those who see may become blind" can be taken of the Jews, who were being blinded by their own unbelief.
How is it that the Saviour says, "The Father is greater than I," and in another place says, "I and the Father are one"?

The Lord Jesus is true man just as he is true God: God from God the Father, man from a human mother. He is believed to have said the first as man and the second as God. By applying this principle of divinity and humanity to the other sayings that speak either of his equality with the Father or of his lowliness, their meaning will readily become clear.

How did the magi offer gifts, as we read: "Opening their treasures, they offered gold, frankincense and myrrh. And having been warned by a divine message in dreams not to go back to Herod, they returned by another road"?

The magi offered gifts to Christ through a foreknowledge given by the Holy Spirit: gold as to a king, frankincense as to God, or else because it pointed to the passion in a figure [?], and myrrh held out a sign of his burial. The magi themselves were a type of believers, while Herod stood as a figure of the devil. The magi were told not to go back to Herod, meaning that those who come to Christ from among the Gentiles must not go back to the devil.
HERE BEGINS ON THE GOSPEL OF MARK.
"The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and the crooked shall be made straight."

The valley he speaks of signifies this world filled with the teaching of Christ. The mountains and hills brought low are the treachery of the devil and the worship of idols, which were humbled and cast down at Christ's coming. When he says, "the crooked shall be made straight," he means the crookedness of the Gentiles, who now walk the straight paths of Christ.
"John's food was locusts and wild honey." How is this to be interpreted?
The locusts he speaks of are a figure of the multitude of people who came to John. The honey signifies the sweet fruit of those whose belief and faith filled John.

"And when Jesus had fasted," it says, "and was afterwards hungry," as the Gospel reading attests: "The tempter said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread.' But Jesus said to him, 'Man does not live by bread, but by every word of God.' Then," it says, "the devil took him, set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, so that the angels may catch you, lest you strike your foot against a stone.'"

These things did indeed happen as history, but in the allegorical sense we must understand [?] ... when the evangelist says. The good tree is the cross, which has borne the fruit of life for believers.

"Everyone who hears my words and does them is like a wise man who built his house on rock. The rain fell, the floods came and beat against that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded on rock," and the rest that follows. What is its meaning?

The rock, of course, is Christ, and the house he speaks of is the dwelling of our body. So let us build our house on this rock, that is, on Christ, so that when the floods and winds come, that is, the assault and storm of persecution, we may be battered but not fall. The sand can only be understood as heresy. Whoever builds his house on this sand, that is, on heresy—his body, that is, and denies his faith [?]—will be a fool, for soon the floods will come, which are the assault of persecution, and at once it will fall.
"See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves."

The wolves are the persecutors, and the sheep are the Christians, who are [?] by the wolves in time of persecution. "But be shrewd," he says, "as serpents." When its life is in danger, the serpent is said to protect its head and give up its body to death. So let us too keep safe our head, that is, Christ, by confessing him, and give up our body to the wolves. The dove is the Church, whose children rejoice whenever they are put to death by men.
"Give to God," he says, "what is God's, and to Caesar what is Caesar's."
In persecution we are commanded to give to Caesar what is Caesar's, that is, the body, over which he has power, and to give to God what is God's, namely the spirit of faith.

"Then," it says, "the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. Five of them were foolish and five were wise. The foolish took their lamps but did not take oil with them in their vessels along with their lamps," and so on.

Of the ten virgins he speaks of, we give five names: hope, faith, love, chastity and almsgiving. The vessels are their dwellings, that is, the people in whom they dwell, which are full of oil, that is, of spiritual grace. The lamps are the watchfulness of the spirit. They go out to meet the bridegroom, that is, Christ. The foolish virgins are the opposites of these: the first, which hopes for what it has seen [?]; the second, unbelief; the third, being without love; the fourth, carnality; the fifth, fruitlessness. Their lamps go out because they have no oil, that is, no spiritual grace.
HERE BEGINS ACCORDING TO LUKE.
"A son will be born to you," it says, "and you will call his name John, and many will rejoice at his birth. He will drink no wine or strong drink."

The wine that John is forbidden to drink is understood as self-indulgence. The strong drink is the juice of dates, which is understood to stand for nothing other than the sweetness of the flesh. For this reason spiritual people avoid this kind of thing altogether.

"In reply," it says, "the Lord Jesus said: 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him, beat him and went off, leaving him behind. Now a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by. Likewise a Levite, when he saw him, passed by too. But a Samaritan was on a journey, and when he came and saw him, he had compassion on him,'" and so on.

Jerusalem means "vision of peace," and Jericho is the world. The man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho is Adam, who was cast out from the presence of God into the world and fell among robbers, that is, into the hands of the devil, who stripped him and inflicted wounds on him. In other words, he took from him the garment of immortality and loaded him with the sins that bring death. By the priest and the Levite we understand Moses and Aaron, who did not tend Adam's wounds, that is, the sins of the Gentiles. The Samaritan is Jesus, for he tended his wounds, that is, he healed our wounds by pouring in wine and oil, the sacrament of his blood and of the chrism. And he brought him to the inn, that is, to the Church, and the innkeepers are the bishops. When he said, "On my return I will repay you," he meant that at his coming he will give the priests their reward.

Jesus said: "A man had two sons. And the younger said, 'Father, give me the share of the property that is mine.' And he divided his property between them. A few days later the younger son gathered everything together and set off for a distant country, and there he squandered his property in loose living," and so on.

In speaking of two sons he introduces a parable about the Gentiles and the Jews. But there is another, deeper meaning, for the two sons are understood as Adam and Christ. The share of the inheritance is paradise, which Adam had received and lost through self-indulgence and disobedience. "He went off," it says, "to a distant country," that is, he was cast out into the world. He ate with the pigs, that is, with the Gentiles. When he came to his senses and returned to his father, this means that the Gentiles, who bore the figure of Adam, came to know their Creator. The robe he was clothed in is the life that the devil had taken from him and that was restored through Christ. "And a ring," it says, "on his hand"—that is, the faith he had lost. The shoes signify feet protected so that they do not fear the devil's snares, as the Apostle says: "your feet shod with the readiness of the gospel." The slaughtered calf is the passion of Christ, who suffered for Adam, that is, for the Gentiles, and to whom the father says, "You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."
ON THE APOSTLE'S LETTER TO THE ROMANS.

How should we understand the passage in which the Apostle says: "But if our wickedness commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust to inflict wrath? I speak in a human way. By no means! Otherwise how will God judge the world? For if through my lie the truth of God has abounded to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner? And why not say, as some slander us and claim that we say, 'Let us do evil so that good may come'? Their condemnation is just."

This is a very obscure and intricate passage in the apostle, and it would need many words to unravel it and bring out its meaning; yet since our discussion must move quickly, we have to treat it briefly. He had said above: "But God is true, and every man a liar, as it is written: that you may be justified in your words and may prevail when you are judged." Then he adds: "But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say?" Here he sifts a question arising from the testimonies he had cited above, and goes on: "Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath," that is, vengeance? "I speak in human terms": that is, according to the human manner of speaking, because he had in a sense called God unjust, or because he had spoken of his wrath, though passion has no place in God. "By no means": that is, far be it from us to believe this, so as to call God unjust if, these things being so, he inflicts wrath on the offender. "Otherwise, how will God judge the world," if not with the highest equity and justice? Then follows: "For if the truth of God has abounded to his glory through my lie." And he puts this forward as one refuting it, not approving it, because if the truth of God needed the lie of man, then neither would the sinner be judged as a sinner, and the slanders spoken against the apostles would appear true. So what is he saying? Even if righteousness shines more brightly by comparison with unrighteousness, man still ought not to be unrighteous so that God may appear righteous. "The condemnation of those who claim that we say these things is just." Say what? "Let us do evil, that good may come." The apostles were thought to say this by those who misinterpreted the apostle's saying, namely: "Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more."

What is meant by what we read: "Why then did Christ, while we were still weak, at the appointed time die for the ungodly? For scarcely will anyone die for a just man; for perhaps for a good man someone might dare to die"?

This is what he wants us to understand: he died for the ungodly, although scarcely anyone can be found who is willing to die for a just man. "For for a good man," that is, for Christ, "perhaps someone might dare to die"; here he also modestly indicates of himself that he could die for Christ. Another interpretation: "For scarcely will anyone die for a just man." Under the old law, in which there is justice in keeping with the severity of the commandments, scarcely a few martyrs were found; but under the New Testament, in which there is goodness in keeping with the kindness of the precepts, countless martyrs have appeared.
The apostle says of God the Father: "But he delivered him up for us all," that is, his Son. What does he mean by this?

"He delivered him up": that is, he consented to his being delivered up. For in the sacred books God is sometimes said to do things in whose doing he is seen to show forbearance. There are some things that God wills to happen, and others that he allows to happen. He wills to happen the things that are evidently better once they are done; but he permits worse things, so that the freedom of human choice may stand firm, and in that freedom of choice a just recompense of their deserts may be rendered by divine judgment to those who pursue good or evil.

In this same epistle, what are we to understand by what we read: "Who shall bring a charge against God's elect? God, who justifies? Who is it that condemns? Christ Jesus, who died, or rather who rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us?"

These words, in which he answers himself, are to be read as if ironically [?]. And the sense is this: unless perhaps either God who justifies or Christ who died for them will condemn his own elect, which by no means will he do who even intercedes for us. So this is what he is saying: no one will condemn the elect.

What are we to think about the passage in which the apostle says: "For I myself could wish to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh," and so on?

"Anathema" sometimes, as here, signifies slaughter and killing. So here the apostle wishes to perish in the flesh so that others may be saved in the spirit. Another interpretation: here the apostle expressed the force of his exceeding

love, wishing, if it were possible, to be accursed from Christ for his brothers, just as Moses did when, interceding with God for his people, he said: "And now, Lord, if you will forgive them their sins, forgive them; but if not, blot me out of your book which you have written."
The same apostle says of God: "So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens." How are we to take this?
The heart is hardened by God when the punishment of its crimes is put off.
Again he states: "What Israel was seeking it did not obtain; but the elect obtained it, and the rest were blinded." What is the meaning of this?

Not that God strikes with blindness anyone who wishes to see, since, as it is written, he wills all to be saved; rather, those who had blinded themselves he is said to have handed over, in requital for their wickedness, when he abandons them. For when the Lord hands over, he forsakes.
How are we to take what is written: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire on his head"?

That is, you heap on him the fire of compunction when you return good for evil. Another interpretation: not that an enemy should be fed with the intention that coals of fire be heaped on his head while he is being fed, but that when that enemy receives good in return for evil and is not moved to any repentance for his malice, it is rather he himself who heaps coals of fire on his own head.
Since there is no authority except from God, as the apostle says, why are not all who wield it found to exercise it well and devoutly?
Because all likewise receive this life equally from God, and yet not all live it equally well.
1 CORINTHIANS

"Every sin," he says, "that a man commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body." How are we to understand this? That other sins are committed by means of the body from outside it, while fornication alone is carried out in the passions of the body itself.
How is that passage to be taken in which it is written: "Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and put to shame those who have nothing?"

Among the Corinthians at one time, as some assert, a perverse custom had taken hold of dishonoring the churches here and there with banquets, at which they ate before the Lord's offering, which they made at night after supper; and since the rich came to the Eucharist drunk, the poor were tormented with hunger. This custom, so they report, came from the superstition of the Gentiles that still lingered. Hence too in certain places in the countryside of Egypt or Syria people are said to gather at church on the night of the Sabbath after supper.

What kind of prophecy is it about which it is written: "But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an outsider comes in, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all, for the secrets of his heart are made manifest"?

Prophecy is of two kinds: one of teaching, the other of foretelling. Foretelling flourished more in past times, teaching in the present. "The secrets of his heart are made manifest" when the conscience of the hearer is pricked as the church prophesies, that is, discourses on how to live.
What is meant by the words: the Son "will deliver the kingdom to God the Father"?

He will deliver it indeed, yet not deliver it in such a way as to be without it. The delivering of the kingdom is our advancement, at the time when we have been found worthy to be sons wholly and entirely in the Father's kingdom.
What is the meaning of the words: "We shall all rise again, but we shall not all be changed"?
That is, we shall not all be changed into glory, because resurrection and incorruption are common to all, but the change into glory belongs properly to the righteous.
2 CORINTHIANS
The apostle says: "We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God. Him who knew no sin he made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him." How are we to take this?

Be reconciled, he says, to God, who made Christ an offering for sin. If you look in the Old Testament, you will find that the offering itself is called "sin." This can also be understood as meaning that Christ was made an offering for sin because God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.
"There was given me," he says, "a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me." How is this to be taken?

Some say that the apostle was often troubled by headaches. But I think it better to take it as meaning that he was buffeted in those sufferings which he himself listed, saying: "Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned," and so on. So by the thorn in the flesh he means the affliction of the flesh, and by the angel of Satan the one at whose instigation, as it were, he suffered such great things.
EPHESIANS

How are we to understand what the apostle writes, that the Lord purposed, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth, in him?

It is truly a wonder what is now restored in heaven. According to the opinion of some, then, that portion of the angels which fell with its prince is restored through the increase and fellowship of the saints, of whom it is written: "but they are like the angels in heaven." All things on earth are restored as well, when believers from the Gentiles are admitted in place of the Jews who fell away. Another interpretation: the things on earth are restored when we are restored through the blood and reconciliation of our Mediator; the heavenly things are restored when joy arises among the angels over our salvation.
What does the apostle mean when he says of God the Father: "from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named"?
Because, since he is our first and true Father, it is from his name that the title is derived when others are called fathers.
How can the apostle say: "Honor your father and mother, which is the first commandment," when among the commandments, as some arrange them, it stands in fourth place?

Some discuss this as follows: the first three commandments all pertain to God, and the following seven to man; the three pertaining to God were contained on one tablet of the law, while on the other tablet were the precepts pertaining to man. So this commandment is the first of the seven commandments that pertain to one's neighbor. Others, however, who maintain that this commandment stands not in fourth but in fifth place (a view we too approve), argue as follows: the whole Decalogue itself, because it was written in that first law, is rightly called the first commandment, since its order certainly makes it first, with the order of the other precepts in the law following afterward. Again, another explanation: "Honor your father and mother, which is the first commandment," and he adds, "with a promise." What promise? "That it may be well with you, and that you may live long on the earth." Therefore, among the commandments this is the first commandment that carries the promise we have just mentioned.
THESSALONIANS
What is the meaning of the words: "Do not quench the Spirit"?
To quench, that is, to drive away by works of wickedness. As David says: "Do not take your Holy Spirit from me."
A little later in the same letter comes: "that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." What are we to understand here?

By "spirit" here he certainly means the Holy Spirit, of whom he had said above: "Do not quench the Spirit." Though he cannot be quenched in his own substance, he is quenched for us when he is taken from us. For his gift or grace in human beings is kindled by their virtues and likewise quenched by their vices. Others assert that "spirit" here should be taken as the understanding and wisdom of the soul itself, of which the same apostle says elsewhere: "And the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God"; that is, the Holy Spirit bears witness to this intellectual spirit of ours that we are children of God. In another place too the apostle says: "I will sing with the spirit, I will sing with the mind also"; here he uses "spirit" for the voice and says that we should sing with voice and mind alike.
COLOSSIANS

What are we to understand in the passage where it is written to the Colossians: "If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though still living in the world, do you lay down rules: 'Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle' — things which all perish in the very using — according to the precepts and teachings of men; which indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility and in not sparing the body, not in any honor, to the satisfying of the flesh"?

Let us touch briefly, as best we can, on a passage wrapped in the deepest obscurity. He is arguing against those Christians from among the Jews who insisted on clinging to their own ceremonies. He had already spoken above about their unacceptable observances in food or drink, and said that their new moons and sabbaths had held out a shadow of things to come. After this, further on, he says again: "If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though still living in the world, do you lay down rules?" — that is, do you pass judgment. What judgment? Namely by saying: "Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle — things which all perish in the very using" (because all those things, he says, which you believe must be neither touched nor tasted perish by their very use, when they are consumed) — "according to the precepts and teachings of men, which indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility and in not sparing the body." He speaks of the teachings of men because those who command that what is forbidden in the law must not be eaten understand the precepts themselves in a carnal way; but this, as he himself adds, consists in superstition and needless humility and in affliction of the body, a body that is not spared either through abstinence of this kind or through circumcision. Then follows: "not in any honor, to the satisfying of the flesh." So this is what he wants understood: all those observances, though they seem to display some practice of wisdom because they are thought to keep the precepts of the law, are nevertheless matters of superstition, not of any honor paid to God, because they are an observance of the flesh serving to fulfil its own will.
1 TIMOTHY
How are we to distinguish each of the things the apostle mentions when he says: "First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made"?

Supplications are made for past or present sins; prayers for obtaining what we hope for; petitions when we intercede for others; thanksgivings when we obtain what we ask, or indeed when we render thanks and praise for God's immense benefits.
How is that passage to be taken in which it is written: "The sins of some men are manifest, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others follow after them"?

He had said above that an accusation against a presbyter should not be received except on the evidence of two or three witnesses, and a little later he added: "The sins of some men are manifest, going before them to judgment," namely when they are known to everyone; "but the sins of others follow after them," namely when they are proven afterward at trial. But if some think this should rather be taken of God's judgment, it can be understood thus: the sins that go before to judgment are those each person has committed here beforehand, while those that follow after are the ones for which we gave the occasion but which are understood to have been brought to completion only after our passing. Sins of this kind, then, follow us to judgment if, for example, someone whose poverty we brought about has been consumed by hunger and want after our death.
2 TIMOTHY
"Alexander the coppersmith," he says, "did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds." And likewise: "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall." How are these to be understood?

He says "will strike you," not "may he strike you," and again "will repay," not "may he repay"; so these words seem to have been spoken not so much in a spirit of cursing as in announcing God's judgment and vengeance. Another interpretation: even if a prophet, in the exercise of his prophetic office, curses with an unmoved mind, as in "Let their eyes be darkened," he is declaring what their deserts require. For every transgression and disobedience receives a just recompense and reward for its deeds.
HEBREWS
How are we to take what the apostle says: "By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph and worshiped the top of his staff"?

By the staff we must understand the meaning of a scepter, and through this of kingship and power: the top, in which Christ is understood to have been worshiped, since he was to be the head of the kingdom of the Hebrews.
ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

What is indicated by what we read: "a sabbath day's journey away"? That is, a thousand paces. On the sabbath the Jews were permitted to go as far as the Mount of Olives; or at any rate, wherever they happened to be, they took it upon themselves to walk that distance.

How is it that, according to the evangelist John, the Holy Spirit is breathed upon the apostles by the Savior before the ascension, when according to the Acts of the Apostles he was sent upon the apostles on the tenth day after the ascension?

There are many gifts of the graces of the Holy Spirit, according to what the apostle says: "To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another the gift of healings in the one Spirit," and so on. So before the ascension they received the grace of the Holy Spirit by which they could forgive sins and baptize and pour the Spirit of adoption into believers; in accordance with which it was said at the time when the Spirit was breathed upon them by the Savior: "Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained." But after the ascension they received a much greater grace of the Holy Spirit, in the working of miracles, the gift of healings, and the receiving of various tongues, in keeping with what had been promised them that same day, that they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit and clothed with power by which they could preach the gospel of Christ to all nations. So in this receiving of the Holy Spirit, according to the Lord's distribution of grace, what is shown is the apostles' progress, not a conflict between the Scriptures. Another explanation of why the Holy Spirit was given twice was excellently set out by a certain teacher, who said of the Spirit whom the Savior first gave here himself and afterward sent from heaven, that this was to signify love of neighbor and love of God, which is poured out in the hearts of the saints through the Holy Spirit who has been given to them.

Which apostles went to which parts of the world to preach the word of God? As far as history relates, Bartholomew went to the Indians, Thomas made his way to the Parthians, Matthew softened the Ethiopians by his preaching and Andrew the Scythians, John set Asia right by the divine word; Peter, while he went about preaching to the Jews of Cappadocia and Galatia, Bithynia as well as Pontus and the neighboring provinces, at last came to Rome to bring it light. Paul, having filled everything from Jerusalem to Illyricum with the gospel, subdued as a victor countless and diverse nations with his precepts as though with weapons.

Since in the Acts of the Apostles we first read: "The men who were traveling with him," that is, with the apostle, "stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one," how is it that the apostle later says: "And those who were with me saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me"?

In the earlier passage, where they are said to have heard a voice from God, what they perceived was not a voice but an inarticulate sound of a voice; so that he afterward says they did not hear the voice, that is, the distinct meaning of the words by which they could understand what was being uttered. And so they are reported on different occasions both to have heard and not to have heard, because as far as the sound is concerned they heard, but as far as the words are concerned they did not.
Why was food that was considered unclean formerly called "common"?

Because, contrary to God's prohibition at that time, it was available in common to the rest of mankind, who did not keep the observance of the law in distinguishing between foods, the observance by which the Jews boasted that they were God's own portion. But it was also purified, as the Lord said to Peter: "What God has cleansed, you must not call common."
What does it mean that in the Acts of the Apostles those twelve who had been baptized with John's baptism are baptized by Paul?

This was because they had not been baptized in the name of the Trinity. For although John baptized into him who was to come, his baptism was nevertheless properly called the baptism of John. Hence also those who come to us from the heretics are not baptized by us if it is established that they were baptized in the name of the Trinity; only the laying on of hands is applied to them when they have turned to the right faith, so that through it they may receive the infusion of the Holy Spirit.
ON THE EPISTLE OF JAMES
How can it be said: "God is no tempter to evil, and he himself tempts no one," when it is nevertheless written: "The Lord your God is testing you"?

The Lord's temptation is called testing. For he tempts no one through the passions; that temptation comes from our own desires, when we are humbled and cast down. The temptation is from the Lord when, having been proved, we are glorified; and so the Lord is no tempter to evil.
ON THE EPISTLE OF JOHN
How does perfect love cast out fear, when it is also written: "The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring for ever and ever"?

Whoever loves God surely dreads being without God. This is the fear of God that endures for ever and ever; this fear, then, comes down from perfect love of the Lord. But that other fear arises from temporal things, whose loss we often dread. It is this fear that the perfection of divine love casts out.
Again, John sets down in his epistle: "There are three that bear witness: the water, the blood, and the spirit." What is indicated by this?

This passage also seems to me to resemble what John himself says in his Gospel about Christ's passion: "One of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out; and he who saw it has borne witness." Earlier in the same Gospel he had said of Jesus: "He bowed his head and gave up his spirit." Some therefore argue from this as follows: the water seems to signify baptism and the blood martyrdom, while the spirit is the spirit itself, which passes to the Lord through martyrdom. Most, however, understand the Trinity itself here by a mystical interpretation, because the perfect Trinity itself bears witness to Christ. The water points to the Father, since he says of himself, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water." The blood shows Christ, through the blood shed in his passion. The spirit reveals the Holy Spirit. These three bear witness to Christ in this way, as he himself says in the Gospel: "I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me has borne witness about me." And again: "But when the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me." So the Father bears witness when he says, "This is my beloved Son"; the Son, when he says, "I and the Father are one"; and the Holy Spirit, when it is said of him, "And he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him."
What does it mean when John says again in his epistle that there is a sin unto death, for which one should not pray?

A sinner surely sins unto death if he does not repent during the course of this temporal life. The saying "But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either here or in the age to come" must be understood in the same way. For a person blasphemes when, refusing to believe the divine promises and the Holy Spirit, in whom is the forgiveness of sins, he declines to be reconciled to God in this life through works of satisfaction.
What does it mean that we read in the same epistle that the world lies in the evil one?

It does not mean that God placed the world in the evil one, but that the vices of the people living in the world are evil. The words of Scripture "because the days are evil" will become clear in the same way.
ON THE APOCALYPSE
Who are the seven spirits of God mentioned in the Apocalypse?

They are the ones the prophet Isaiah also lists: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and truth, and the spirit of the fear of God. In them, however, spiritual works are signified. But one and the same Spirit works all these things.

These, then, are the things I have set out at your request from the opinions of the most learned men. If, however, anyone should bring forward in the discussion of these questions views that are more convincing, rejecting the stubbornness so common in most people, I do not refuse to follow what is better.
BOOK TWO

My dearest son, in the previous book I gave answer after answer to your questions, and I fear that a constant series of questions may, as often happens, weary the reader until he grows bored. So now, to vary the work, I will add in my own name the things I had promised, dividing each of them into its categories and placing them under their own headings, so that the very arrangement may make them clearer. First I will come to the interpretation of Hebrew names, and for brevity's sake I will give only those that are certain and better known.

Adonai means "Lord" in Latin. Sabaoth: "of hosts" or "of powers," or, as some prefer, "almighty." Jesus: "savior." Nazarene: "holy." Messiah: "anointed," that is, Christ. Michael: "who is like God." Gabriel: "strength of God." Raphael: "medicine of God." Adam: "man" or "earth-born." Eve: "life" or "calamity." I wonder why the Hebrews interpret this name in such different ways, unless perhaps because she brought man life by giving birth and calamity by transgressing, or because a woman is sometimes life to some and calamity to others. Abel: "mourning" or "pitiable." Cain: "possession" or "lamentation." Enoch: "dedication." Methuselah: "he died and sent." Noah: "rest." Shem: "named." Ham: "hot." Japheth: "breadth." Lot: "turning aside" or "bound." Melchizedek: "righteous king." Abram: "exalted father." Abraham: "father seeing the people" or "father of many," that is, of nations. Sarai: "my princess." Sarah: "princess." Note that to both names, Abraham's and Sarah's, the Lord added only the letter a, which among the Hebrews, however, is read as e. Hagar: "stranger" or "converted." Ishmael: "hearing of God." Isaac: "laughter"; yet he was not so called, as some think, because Sarah laughed, but because of Abraham, who is shown to have laughed first at that time. Rebecca: "patience" or "she who has received much." Jacob: "supplanter." Israel: "a man seeing God," but better, "prince with God." Leah: "laborious." Rachel: "ewe" or "seeing God." Reuben: "seeing son" or "seeing in the midst." Simeon: "one who hears sorrows." Levi: "joined" or "added." Judah: "confessing" or "glorifying." Zebulun: "dwelling of beauty." Issachar: "there is reward." Dan: "judgment" or "judging." Gad: "temptation." Asher: "breadth" or "blessed." Naphtali: "turning." Benjamin: "son of the right hand." Ephraim: "fruitful" or "abundance," or in Latin "Augentius." Manasseh: "forgotten." Esau: "oaken [?]" or "heap of stones." Kedar: "darkness" or "grief." Job: "great" or "grieving." Amalek: "a people licking up" or "quenching." Moses: "taking up" or "anointing." Aaron: "mountain of strength." Pharaoh: "stripping him bare" or "his destroyer." But Pharaoh is the name not of a man but of a rank, just as among us emperors are called Augustus, although they are listed under their own names. Yet the Pharaoh who was drowned in the Red Sea was called by his own name Cenchres. Joshua: "savior." Othniel: "his time is God" or "the answer of God." Ehud: "glorious." Shamgar: "name of a stranger" or "a settler there." Barak: "lightning." Deborah: "bee" or "talkative." Gideon: "temptation of their iniquity." Abimelech: "my father is king." Tola: "little worm" or "scarlet." Jair: "enlightening." Jephthah: "opening" or "opened." Ibzan: "thought" or "girdle of grief." Elon: "living to God" or "seeing God." Abdon: "his servant." Samson: "their sun" or "strength of the sun." Delilah: "poor little woman" or "bucket." Eli: "my God." Samuel: "his name is God." Saul: "sought after" or "request." Jesse: "burnt offering of the island" or "sacrifice." David: "desirable" or "strong of hand." Jonathan: "gift of the dove" or "gift of the Lord." Absalom: "father of peace." Solomon: "peaceable"; he is also Ecclesiastes, that is, "the preacher," and also Jedidiah, that is, "beloved of the Lord." Rehoboam: "breadth of the people." Abijah: "the Lord is father." Asa: "lifting" or "raising up." Jehoshaphat: "judgment of the Lord." Joram: "who is exalted." Ahaziah: "taking hold of the Lord." Athaliah: "time of the Lord." Joash: "hoping" or "temporal." Amaziah: "lifting the people." Uzziah: "strength of the Lord." Azariah: "help of the Lord." Jotham: "he is perfect." Ahaz: "taking hold." Hezekiah: "strength of the Lord." Manasseh: "forgetful" or "what has he forgotten." Amon: "faithful" or "foster-father." Josiah: "where is the incense" or "salvation of the Lord." Jehoahaz: "robust." Jehoiakim: "whose is the preparation." Eliakim: "resurrection of God." Jeconiah: "preparation of God." Zedekiah: "righteous one of the Lord." Jeroboam: "judging the people" or "judging those above." Nadab: "barking." Baasha: "fatness." Elah: "of the age" or "of the world." Zimri: "psalm" or "my song." Omri: "my curling." Ahab: "father's brother." Jezebel: "flowing with blood" or "where is the dunghill." Ahaziah: "taking hold of the Lord." Joram: "who is exalted," but better, "he will be lifted up." Jehu: "he himself" or "he is." Joatha [?]: "robust." Zechariah: "mindful of the Lord." Shallum: "his shadow" or "request." Menahem: "consoling." Pekahiah: "opening." Elijah: "of the Lord God." Elisha: "salvation of my God." Hosea: "savior." Joel: "God beginning" or "he is God." Amos: "powerful" or "strong," or "tearing away the people." Obadiah: "servant of the Lord." Jonah: "dove" or "grieving." Micah: "who is this." Nahum: "sprout" or "consolation." Habakkuk: "embracing." Zephaniah: "hiding her." Haggai: "festive" or "solemn." Zechariah: "mindful of the Lord." Malachi: "my angel." Isaiah: "the Lord's alone." Jeremiah: "exalted one of the Lord." Ezekiel: "strength of the Lord." Daniel: "judgment of God." Judith: "praising," or "Jewess." Joseph: "increased." Mary: "enlightened" or "star of the sea," but in Syriac "lady." Simon: "put away sorrow" or "obedient." Peter: "acknowledging." Bar-Jonah: "son of the dove," a word that is both Syriac and Hebrew. Cephas: "Peter"; it is Syriac. Paul: "wonderful." Saul: "temptation of one looking back" or "security." Andrew: "manly"; it is Greek. James: "supplanter." John: "grace of the Lord." Philip: "mouth of lamps." Bartholomew: "son of him who holds up the waters." Thomas: "abyss" or "twin," which is why he is also called Didymus in Greek. Matthew: "given"; he was also called Levi. Lebbaeus: "little heart," that is, from "heart"; he is also Thaddaeus, and also Judas son of James. Cananaean: "possessing" or "possession"; Simon was so called from the village of Cana, and he is also the Zealot. Iscariot: "memorial of the Lord" or "memory of death"; Judas was called by this name from the village in which he was born. Mark: "exalted in command." Luke: "himself rising up" or "himself lifting up." Stephen: "your rule," but in Greek "crowned." Pontius: "turning aside from counsel." Pilate: "mouth of the hammerer." Barabbas: "son of their master," no doubt the master of the Jews, who is the devil. Eden, in Genesis: "delights." Judea: "confession." Jerusalem: "vision of peace." Zion: "watchtower," and rightly so, for this city of David was built on a mountain. Babylon: "confusion" or "removal." Ethiopia: "darkness." Egypt: "tribulation" or "darkness." Tyre: "distress." Romans: "lofty" or "thundering." Rhome: "strength"; it is Greek. Sinai: "measure" or "command," or "temptation," or "my jar." Gehenna: "the free valley"; some think it was named after the valley of Gehennom, which is next to the wall of Jerusalem. Hebrews: "those who pass over." Sadducees: "justified." Pharisees: "separated." Galileans: "turning" or "changeable." Samaritans: "guards," because the Babylonians stationed them there to keep watch over the Jews.

This shows clearly, as so many other things do, how truly divine and full of mysteries the whole of sacred Scripture is, since its names so fit the facts and correspond to the outcomes. David, for instance, whose name means "strong of hand" in Latin, proved himself the strongest of all in almost every war. Solomon, "peaceable," governed his kingdom in peace. Daniel, "judgment of God," delivered a verdict of divine discernment in the judgment of the elders. So is it any wonder that these men prophesied the future, when, as the facts show, even their names speak prophecy? But let us now give the interpretation of various other words.

Alleluia means "praise the Lord" in Latin, for Ia is one of the ten names of God found among the Hebrews. Amen: "truly" or "faithfully." Diapsalma: "always," that is, it confirms that the things to which it is attached are made everlasting by God. It does not mean a change of meter, as some think, or a pause to refresh the prophetic spirit. There are also some who think diapsalma is written to show that there is a change either of speakers or of thought. Hosanna: "save" or "bring salvation." For Osi means "save," and anna is an interjection of entreaty, so in full it is said Osianna; but when it is shortened or corrupted it sounds Hosanna. The sense is "bring salvation," with either the people of Israel or the whole world understood. Rama: "on high"; in the Gospel, "A voice was heard in Rama," that is, on high. There is, however, also a city called Rama. Raca: "empty" or "worthless." Rabbi: "my master"; it is Syriac. Abba: "father"; this too is Syriac. Man: "what?" Manna: "what is this?" Anathema: "perdition." Maranatha: "our Lord has come"; it is Syriac. Anathema Maranatha, as some say, means "perdition at the coming of the Lord." Mammon: "riches." Teraphim: "figures" or "images," which is a better rendering than "burnings." Seraphim or Seraphin: "burning" or "setting on fire," in keeping with the verse "who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire." So they affirm that the Seraphim are powers in heaven who praise God and are sent on various ministries. Cherubim: "fullness of knowledge." In the holy of holies itself, however, the cherubim signify only two living creatures; in other places where this name is read, it indicates some kind of picture or ornamentation.

Mandrake, in Genesis: a kind of fruit very like a small melon in appearance and smell. Mazzaroth, in Job: the zodiac signs, which the astrologers say are twelve. Fath: klima, that is, a region, such as the south or the west. Rhamnus, in the Psalter, is not a bramble but a kind of thornbush with very troublesome briars. Rhomphaea means "sword" in Latin, for where Genesis speaks of a flaming and turning sword, the Greek has rhomphaea. Frameae are very long spears; the Armoricans, who still use them, give them this name. Some think swords are also meant by it. Caper, in Solomon: a kind of shrub in the East, like the mastic tree. Palathae, in Kings: cakes that are usually pressed together from fresh figs; palathae is Greek. Debelaim, in the prophet Hosea, they say means palathae. Dabir, in Kings: the oracle, which was made in the middle of the inner part of the temple, where the ark of the Lord also was; it was called the holy of holies. Byssus: a kind of silk, coarser and also stronger. Phoenicium, in Isaiah: scarlet. Lavers, in Kings: basins or water jars; cantharus is also a Greek word. Latomi, in Kings: stonecutters; this too is Greek. Kreagrae, in Chronicles: forks for taking meat out of cauldrons; it is Greek. Sambucae: in music, a kind of instrument for playing together. The nablum, which in Greek is called the psaltery and is named from "psallein," to play, is like a barbarian lyre, shaped like the letter delta. The tympanum is made of stretched skin or leather. Cinari, as some think, are small bowls that, when struck, are set ringing in rhythm. Thyine wood: from this Solomon made the steps in the house of the Lord; it is a wood unknown even to the more learned Jews. Shittim, in the Pentateuch: a kind of thornbush in the desert, from which comes wood that does not rot. Sabeth is the Hebrew word for a thicket; in Genesis it says: "Behold, a ram behind him was caught in the thicket Sabeth." Lebetes: small bronze cauldrons made for cooking, in Chronicles: "But they cooked the peace offerings in lebetes and pots and pans." Cophinus: a basket. Hydria: a water jar. Condi, in Genesis: a cup or goblet. Lecythus, in Kings: an oil flask. Lenticula, in the book of Kings: a small bronze vessel holding the oil with which men were anointed king. Parapsis: a larger dish; some think a platter is also called this. Epistylia, in Kings: what is placed on top of the capitals of columns; it is Greek. Mechonoth, in Kings: supports, which we call bases. Topaz: a precious stone in which, as some affirm, the colors of all stones shine. Corban: the treasury; Corbona, however, means "offering." Chasma, in Luke: a gulf; it is Greek. Erysibe, in the prophet: blight, that is, rust on the crops; it is Greek. Zizania: darnel. Sicera: juice from dates; and every drink other than wine that is made for drinking from fruit or anything else is called sicera. Nard pistic: faithful nard, that is, unadulterated; it is Greek. Spikenard, so called because the kind of nard from which the ointment is made by infusion is shaped like an ear of grain. Alabaster: a kind of precious marble, from which the little jar of that ointment in the Gospel was made. Stadium, in the Gospel: a fixed measure of distance; eight stadia make a mile.

The following words are found in Exodus and in the books of Kings, in the passages that describe the ark, the tabernacle or the temple of the Lord. Of these words, the more obscure terms are those found in the old translation; the ones that appear clearer are contained in the text of the new translation.

So where the old translation has speroteres, the new has "rods"; for calamisci, "reeds"; for troisci or carisci, "shaped somewhat like nuts"; for anconisci, "joints"; for aspidicae, "hooks"; for fimbriae, "little chains"; for scytalae, "bars"; for acrotomic stones, "hewn stones"; for degraphis, "carving"; for petala, "plates"; for perimetrum, "line"; for spirae, "the capitals of the columns," or, as I think, "their workmanship"; for aelam, "porch," though it is better interpreted as "before the doors" or "vestibule"; aelam, then, is Hebrew. The other terms above are mostly Greek. Likewise, at the end of Ezekiel, in the vision of the city, the old translation has pastophoria, the new "treasuries," that is, small chambers; for thee, "chambers"; for aileu, "front"; for aelaumoth, "vestibule"; for polyandrium, "multitudes"; for spithame, "handbreadth"; for gissus, "boundary"; for manaa, "sacrifice." In Kings, cenotaphia are images, which in Greek are morphomata. But enough of this. Now learn also what Scripture first called certain peoples and what they are called now.

Gomer, in Genesis: the Galatians, that is, the Gauls, who were first called Galatians from the whiteness of their bodies. Peoples from among them once migrated to the far reaches of the East and were at first called Gallo-Greeks, but are now called Galatians by the ancient name of the Gauls. Magog: the Scythians; some think Gog and Magog are the Goths. Tubal: the Iberians, who are also the Spaniards.

Tiras: the Thracians. Togarmah: the Phrygians. Madai: the Medes. Javan: the Ionians, who are also the Greeks, from whom the Ionian Sea is named. Kittim: the Citians, that is, the Cypriots, among whom there is also a city called Citium. Dodanim: the Rhodians. From these came the Greek nations that occupied the seacoast from the Taurus mountains to the western Ocean. All these nations are descended from the stock of Japheth.

Cush: Ethiopia. Mizraim: Egypt. Casluhim: those who were later called Philistines and are now Palestinians; they were also called Allophyli, that is, foreigners. Their city is Ashkelon. Seba: Arabia; Saba is also the name of a region where the Sabaeans now live. Havilah: the Gaetulians. Lehabim: now the Libyans; they were once called Phutaeans. Tarshish, or Carchedon, is Carthage; some think Tarshish refers to the Cilicians, because the city of Tarsus is located there. Africa was named after one of Abraham's descendants by Keturah, who was called Afer. The Ishmaelites were named after Ishmael, son of Abraham; they are also called Saracens, from Sarah, and Hagarenes, from Hagar. The Nabataeans, named after Nebaioth, son of Ishmael, extend from the Euphrates to the Red Sea. The Canaanites were named after Canaan, son of Ham; the Jews drove out the inhabitants and took possession of their land. These come from the line of Ham. Asshur: the Assyrians, from Asshur, son of Shem; they founded the city of Ninus, named after King Ninus, which is now called Nineveh. Some claim that the Syrians were named after Asshurim, son of Abraham by Keturah. Uz: the region of Ausitis, around Coele-Syria, so named after Uz, the great-grandson of Shem. The Elamites, that is, the Persians, from Elam, son of Shem. The Hebrews were named after Eber, who was the great-grandson of Shem. The Chasdim are now called Chaldeans; they were called Chasdim after Chesed, son of Nahor, Abraham's brother. All these descend from the posterity of Shem.

Jebus is Jerusalem, and it is also Salem, where Melchizedek reigned. It is now called Aelia, after Aelius Hadrian. Babel in Genesis is now called Babylon. In this place, when men once set out to build a tower against heaven, they were scattered after God sent a confusion of tongues. Accad is now called Nisibis. Riblah is now called Antioch, and it is also Epiphania. Shechem is also Sicima, and it is now Neapolis, the city of the Samaritans. Oholibamah in the prophet is a city in which the princes of Edom lived. Ariel in Isaiah: some think this is Areopolis, named after the idol of Mars, Ariel, which stands there. But Ariel means "lion of God," and figuratively signifies Jerusalem. Ararat is Armenia, on whose mountains the ark came to rest after the flood, so that some traces of it remain there even now. Arbe, which is corruptly read as Arbos in our manuscripts, is where three patriarchs are buried, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Adam himself besides; this is also Hebron, where David reigned. Lod is Lydda, and also Diospolis. Decapolis in the Gospel is a region with ten cities. Ekron is a city of Palestine; there are others who think that Ekron is Strato's Tower and that it was later called Caesarea. Antilebanon is the name given to the places beyond Mount Lebanon that face the eastern region. Ephrathah is the district of the city of Bethlehem, whereas the Euphrates is a river from paradise. Mesopotamia is so called because it is surrounded by the rivers Tigris and Euphrates. Emmaus in the Gospel was once the name of a fortified village; it is now a city called Nicopolis. The place of Calvary was so called because condemned men were customarily beheaded there. Areopagus is the name of a council of the Athenians, which took its name from Mars.

Gihon is a river of Ethiopia that rises from paradise, commonly called the Nile. Pishon is a river of India that also flows from paradise; others call it the Ganges. The Jordan is so called because two springs flow together into one, one called Jor and the other Dan. The Sea of Galilee is the same as the Sea of Tiberias, the Lake of Gennesaret, and the Lake of Chinnereth. The Salt Sea is also called the Dead Sea or the Sea of Asphalt, that is, of bitumen; it is not far from Jericho. Bethsaida is a pool in Jerusalem into which the sick were carried. It is also called Probatica, that is, "of the flock," because the priests once washed the sacrificial victims in it.

Nisan in the book of Esther is the month they call March, which in the scriptures is called the first month. Elul in the book of Maccabees is August, which we call the sixth month. Chislev in the prophet Zechariah is November, which is also the ninth. Tebeth in the book of Esther is December, which is also the tenth. Shebat in the prophet Zechariah is January, which for us is the eleventh. Adar in the book of Esther is February, which for us is the twelfth. And if you also want to know the remaining Hebrew names of the months, which I did not find in the canon: the second month is called Iyyar, the third Sivan, the fourth Tammuz, the seventh Tishri, the eighth Marheshvan.

The year of jubilee is the fiftieth year, which was the year of release, in which everyone in Israel who had sold his property regained his right to it, even without paying a price. Pascha means "passing over"; the word is Hebrew, not Greek. It is called "passing over" because the Hebrews passed over from Egypt into the land of promise; and our Pascha is surely this, that the Savior, rising from the underworld, passed over into the kingdom of heaven. Phase is likewise Pascha, a passing over or crossing. Some maintain rather that it was called a passing over or crossing because on that same night the Lord passed through Egypt when he struck down all the firstborn of the Egyptians. Pentecost means "fiftieth"; it is Greek. The year of jubilee bore the figure of this fiftieth, which now in turn prefigures the eternal rest of the promise to come. Scenopegia is when tents are pitched by the Jews in memory of the tents, for in Greek σκήνη means tent. This feast of the Jews is celebrated in the month of September. Encaenia is the observance or dedication of a new building, for kainon in Greek means new; so at this feast in the month of October the Jews kept the day of the dedication of the temple. Epiphany is Greek and means appearing or showing, either because on that day our Lord and Savior was shown to the people at his baptism, or because the star appeared to the Magi, or because the water turned into wine then appeared as the Lord's first sign. Neomenia is what we call the Kalends. But since among the Hebrews the months are reckoned by the course of the moon, and in Greek the moon is called ΜΗΝΗ, Neomenia can be taken to mean "new moon." Parasceve means preparation; it is Greek, for the sixth day of the week is called Parasceve. It is called preparation because on that day the Jews prepare what is needed for the Sabbath. Sabbath means rest; it is Hebrew. It is called rest because on that day the Lord rested from his work, when everything had been completed and finished.

Idols means images; it is Greek. Baal-peor, which means "image of shame," is an idol. Mob: the Latins call him Priapus. Bel, which means "antiquity," is a Babylonian idol; he was the same Belus who was father of Ninus, king of the Assyrians. Adrammelech is an idol of the Assyrians, which the Samaritans also worshipped. Astarte, which in Latin means "superfluous making," is said to be an idol of the Sidonians. Beelzebub means "man of flies." Diabolus means "flowing down," but in Greek it means "accuser." Satan in Latin means "adversary" or "transgressor." The sirens in Isaiah are demons, or great serpents that are both crested and winged, as some think.

The howlers in Isaiah are called in every translation by the Hebrew name itself, Ihihim; only the Seventy translators put "onocentaurs" in their place. Some think the howlers are night birds, named after the howling cry they utter, which are commonly called cavanni. The lamia in Isaiah is a kind of monster, as some maintain. The hairy ones in Isaiah are kinds of demons; some, even among the most learned, have thought they should be understood as incubi, or satyrs, or certain wild men of the woods.

The ephod is a priestly garment which is called an overgarment or superhumeral. It is something like a caracalla, but without a hood. There are two kinds of this garment: one of plain linen, which the priests wore, and another woven of various colors with gold and gems, which only the high priests used. The poderes is a priestly linen garment fitting closely to the body and reaching to the ankles, which is why it is called poderes; it is also called the undertunic. The logium, also called the rationale, is a small cloth of gold, gems and various colors, which was fastened to the superhumeral over the high priest's breast.

The cidaris is a priestly cap of fine linen; the Greeks and our own people call it a tiara, and some also call it a mitre. The petalum is a gold plate on the high priest's forehead which bore inscribed that ineffable name of God, the tetragrammaton, that is, the name of four Hebrew letters. The paenula in the Apostle is a Latin word; it is a kind of cloak with stripes running down it. The diplois in Kings is a military cloak, a chlamys, from ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΔΙΠΛΟΥΣΘΑΙ, because it is doubled; any garment that wraps us twice over can be called a diplois. Baddim in Daniel are linen garments, by which, I think, breeches are meant. For among the Hebrews bad means linen. Hence in some places we read "ephod bad," that is, a linen ephod, and not "ephod barut," as some corruptly read. The melote in Kings is a single skin, hanging down from one side, which Egyptian monks still use even now. The theristrum in Genesis is a kind of women's mantle among the Arabs. Periscelides in Isaiah are, as some say, ornaments worn by women on their legs.

The pelican is a small bird that delights in solitude. There is also another kind of pelican on the Nile, almost like swans except that they are a little larger; some also call these onocrotali. The nycticorax is the night owl; many contend that it is the horned owl, and there are also those who assert that it is an eastern bird called the night raven. The ibis in the Pentateuch is an Egyptian bird, unclean because of the foulness of its beak, which it uses to purge its bowels. The herodius in the psalm is thought by some to be the heron. Larus in the Pentateuch means the gull. Coenomyia in the psalm should be understood not as "dog-fly," as some think, but as "fly of every kind," and so it should be spelled not with the Greek letter y but with the diphthong oe. Sciniphes are a kind of gnat, very troublesome with their stings.

The rhinoceros is a fearsome beast that bears two horns on its nose. The monoceros in the psalm is called the unicorn. The tragelaphus in Deuteronomy is the platyceros, that is, the broad-horned. The erinacei are called ΧΟΙΡΟΓΡΥΛΛΟΙ; they are about the size of middling rabbits, and they come out of caves in the rocks and graze in herds in the desert that faces the Dead Sea. The ericii, which are called ΕΧΙΝΟΙ, are so protected by a spiny covering that they cannot even be touched. Bruchus in the psalm means locusts that cannot yet fly. Eruca is what is commonly called dolua.

A talent weighs sixty-two and a half pounds, which makes eighty Attic pounds. A mina is one pound and a half-ounce. A talent has sixty minas. In Greek it is called mna, in Latin mina. A drachma has three scruples; a didrachma is two drachmas, so I wonder how a half-ounce came to be written in the book of Hebrew Questions. A stater is a coin that weighs, as some assert, one ounce, that is, six gold pieces, or, as others think, three; for in the Gospel a stater is paid in place of two didrachmas. The shekel, which in Latin is corruptly called siclus, as is shown in the Questions mentioned above, has the weight of an ounce; as I have found written elsewhere, it is ten scruples, which I myself also think. For siclus or shekel sounds like sicilicus because they are close in weight. An obol is half a scruple, which makes three siliquae, in Ezekiel; and the shekel has twenty obols.

A cor is thirty modii. A bath is one amphora, that is, three modii. A cadus is a Greek amphora and holds three urns. An ephi or ephah is three modii. The ephah holds the same amount in dry measure as the bath does in liquid measure. One metretes, as some say, holds a hundred sextarii; in Greek a measure is called ΜΕΤΡΟΝ, which is why it is called metretes. But note that "measure" is a Hebrew name. Artabae in Isaiah are Egyptian measures, three of which make ten modii. Sata are the same as the ephah, that is, three modii. An omer is an Attic measure holding, as some think, three choenices, that is, twelve sextarii; others say an omer is a little less than five sextarii, and I follow this view myself, because an omer is the tenth part of an ephah. Some think a nebel is three modii. A sextarius is a liquid measure. A cotyla is a hemina, in Ezekiel: "Ten cotylae," it says, "make an omer."
Now take the meanings of those names which are used in the speech of the Church and have been brought over into our language from Greek.

Theos means God; and theos, as some hold, comes from ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΘΕΑΣΕΣΘΑΙ, from seeing, that is, from looking out over all things. Homoousion means of one substance. Homoiousion means of like substance. Christ means anointed. The Spirit Paraclete means the Spirit who consoles, or the advocate. Hagios means holy. Angel means messenger. Throne means seat or royal chair. Apostle means one sent, because they were sent by the Lord to preach the gospel, although teachers think the word is Hebrew. Prophet means one who foretells. Martyrs means witnesses. Bishop means overseer, and so the prophet says: "I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel." Presbyter means elder. Deacon means minister. Clergy means lot. Church means a calling out or gathering. Catholic means universal, from ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΚΑΘ' ΟΛΟΝ, that is, according to the whole. Synagogue means assembly or congregation. Ethnicus means gentile. Hypocrite means pretender. Heresy means sect. Monk means solitary. Hermitage (eremus) means desert. Parish (paroecia) means the house next door, that is, God's. Diocese means government, and this not according to the proper or literal force of the word but according to its effect. Layman means one of the people, from ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΛΑΟΥ. Catechumen means one instructed, or a hearer. Neophyte means a new planting. Baptistery means a place of dipping. Chrism means anointing. Eucharist means grace. Holocaust means wholly burnt, because the whole victim was given over to the fire and consumed. Symbol means a contribution, or a covenant or agreement that man has with God. Hymn means a song in praise of God. Antiphon means a voice answering back. Pentateuch means five volumes, that is, the five books of Moses, which is why the Apostle says that he would rather speak five words in the church. Exodus means going out or departure, that is, of the people of Israel. Deuteronomy means second law, in which there is a prefiguring of the law of the Gospel. Paralipomenon means of things left out or remaining, that is, because it contains histories that were left out of the books of Kings. Gospel means good announcement or good news. Apocalypse means revelation. Gazophylacium means guardian of riches, a compound of Persian and Greek. Synod means company or assembly. Canon means rule. Teuchos means volume, hence Pentateuch. Apocrypha means hidden or secret. Hexapla means sixfold. Apology means defense, hence the name apologeticus. Anagoge means the higher sense. Tropology means moral understanding. Parable means likeness.

Here you have, my dearest son, a little work covering almost the whole body of the scriptures, a kind of seedbed of understanding. In these two volumes I have gathered, I think, no small amount of instruction from various and necessary subjects to teach you.
